add.issue.name: Unreadable-event lock silently no-ops when the target is not a materialized node

edit.description.md:
From an architectural review of `fix/z8npac8-schema-version-compat` (commit 6a14a53).

`applyUnreadableLocks` (`source/lib/event/event-boot.ts`) discards `markNodeUnreadable`'s `Result`. When `targetNodeId` names something absent from `state.nodes`, no lock lands — and the board-wide fallback does not fire either, because the filter is `!event.targetNodeId` and the id *was* present.

Two ways in, both verified by probe:

- The unreadable event is what **created** the node. A `v:2` `add.issue` + `v:2` `edit.title` for ticket `tFuture` reports `targetNodeId: "tFuture"`, then boot succeeds with `readOnly: false`, parent swimlane and board unlocked, and `tFuture` absent. A whole ticket is invisible and the board fully writable, with no warning.
- The id is not a node at all — `create.tag`, `create.contributor`, a comment id. Same silent no-op.

Fix: treat a failed `markNodeUnreadable` as unlocalizable and fold it into the board-wide set, so the fallback covers the case it was designed for.

Also tighten `getTargetNodeId`: it takes the first object-valued key's `.id`, but the "exactly one payload key" invariant `getPersistedAction` enforces is never checked on this path, and `.id` semantics vary (`add.issue.comment.id` is the comment, not the issue). Ambiguity should return null rather than guess.

add.issue.name: Every path back to live drops the unreadable-event locks

edit.description.md:
From an architectural review of `fix/z8npac8-schema-version-compat` (commit 6a14a53).

`bootStateFromEventLog` is one of four routes to live state and the only one that applies the load-derived locks. The other three rebuild the node graph with `resetState()` → `materializeAll()` → `patchState({readOnly: false})`, bypassing it entirely:

- `restoreLiveState` (`source/mcp/epiq-time-travel.ts`) — backs `returnToLive` and the failure recovery path
- `:peek now` (`source/lib/command-line/commands/peek.cmd.ts`)
- `finishReplay` (`source/lib/command-line/commands/replay-engine.ts`)

Per-node locks are applied post-materialize by `applyUnreadableLocks`, which those paths never call, and the board-wide `readOnly` is explicitly cleared. So peek-then-return hands back a fully writable board over a log this build cannot read — the exact failure the locking exists to prevent, two keystrokes away.

Related: those `patchState` calls do not clear `readOnlyReason`, so it survives `readOnly: false`. Enter peek afterwards and `materializeAndPersistAll` quotes the stale "cannot read N events… Upgrade epiq" instead of the time-travel message.

Fix: one shared re-lock the live transitions all call, sourced from the last full load.

add.issue.name: readonlyReason is computed and plumbed through, then discarded at every surface

edit.description.md:
From an architectural review of `fix/z8npac8-schema-version-compat` (commit 6a14a53).

The branch adds `NavNode.readonlyReason` so a load-derived lock can explain itself. Nothing reads it — the only reference outside the type is `node-repo.ts` setting it.

- `failIfReadonly` returns fixed strings ("Cannot edit readonly node")
- `epiq-api` mutation guards return fixed strings ("Cannot edit readonly issue", ×11)
- The MCP and GUI node projections emit `readonly: Boolean(n.readonly)` and drop the reason

So a user hits a locked ticket with no way to learn it is locked because their build cannot read part of its history, which is the entire point of the field. Either surface it end to end or drop it.

add.issue.name: The stable event envelope has a closed id tuple, so extending id bricks old clients

edit.description.md:
From an architectural review of `fix/z8npac8-schema-version-compat` (commit 6a14a53).

`PersistedEnvelopeSchema` is the branch's forward-compatibility contract: `v` + `id` are declared stable across every schema version so ancestry stays readable on a line whose payload is not. But it reuses `CompositeIdSchema`, which is `z.tuple([string, string|null])`, and zod 4 tuples reject extra elements (verified).

So the day a version appends a third element to `id` — a vector clock, a second parent for a merge — every older client hard-fails `parsePersistedEnvelope` → `parsePersistedEventsFile` → the whole board is unloadable. That is Z8NPAC8 again, relocated from `v` to `id`.

The envelope promises stability but its one structured field is closed. `.rest(z.unknown())` on an envelope-specific id schema makes the promise real; the write-side `PersistedEventSchema` should stay strict, since `toPersistedEvent` builds a 2-tuple itself.

add.issue.name: SCHEMA_VERSION is not linked to READABLE_SCHEMA_VERSIONS, so a bump can ship unreadable

edit.description.md:
From an architectural review of `fix/z8npac8-schema-version-compat` (commit 6a14a53).

`READABLE_SCHEMA_VERSIONS` carries the comment "Listed literally so a bump that forgets to add itself fails at once instead of on someone else's machine." There is no such link — the set is a plain `Set<number>` with no relation to `SCHEMA_VERSION`.

Bump `SCHEMA_VERSION` to 2 without touching the set and it type-checks fine. Every event the build writes is then skipped when it reads its own log back, and it surfaces at runtime, only on a non-empty log, as `"Initialized Epiq project has no workspace init event"` — a message that points nowhere near the cause.

A compile-time assert that `SCHEMA_VERSION` is a member makes the comment true.

add.issue.name: Contributor-authorship guards read only the events this build can decode

edit.description.md:
From an architectural review of `fix/z8npac8-schema-version-compat` (commit 6a14a53).

`tombstoneContributor` refuses removal for anyone who has authored an event, because the log names them throughout and is never rewritten. Its guard, `findEventLogAuthor`, and the `hasAuthoredAnywhere` projection both scan `loadMergedEvents`, which now silently drops events this build cannot decode.

So a contributor whose only authorship lives in unreadable events looks unauthored, the guard clears, and a `tombstone.contributor` is written on a false premise. Pre-existing for unknown actions; the branch widens it to whole schema versions.

The actor does not need decoding — `parseEventFileActor` derives `userId`/`userName` from the file name, which no payload version can make unreadable. These guards should read actors off the envelopes, not the decoded log.

Note contributor ids are not nav nodes, so the per-node lock does not cover them either (see the localization ticket).

Out of scope: `findCreatedContributorName` reads `create.contributor` *payloads*, so it genuinely needs decoding and degrades to `undefined` for an unreadable version. That is inherent, not fixable here.

add.issue.comment.md:

add.issue.name: Decide where the unreadable-event diagnostics should live

edit.description.md:
Needs your call — I picked an option to unblock 5R0J7DV and want it confirmed or changed.

Three paths return to live (`:peek now`, `returnToLive`, end of replay) by `resetState()` → `materializeAll()` → reopen writes. They must re-derive the load-time unreadable locks afterwards, which means reading the diagnostics on the far side of a reset that wipes `AppState`.

**What I shipped (commit 0de3075):** a module-level `lastUnreadable` in `event-load.ts`, written by `loadMergedEventsWithDiagnostics` and read by `relockUnreadableEvents()`.
- No extra disk read; refreshed by every full load; derived only, never persisted
- But it is hidden global state. It cannot go stale in practice (each live path loads immediately before re-locking, and `finishReplay` is TUI-only so it is always the same repo), though nothing in the type system says so. A single MCP process serving two repos is the theoretical leak; today no such caller exists.

**Alternative A — re-derive from disk.** `relockUnreadableEvents(stateBranchRoot)` calls `loadMergedEventsWithDiagnostics` itself. No cached state, impossible to go stale, matches "state is derived by replaying". Costs a second full log read on each transition, and `finishReplay` would need a state-branch root it does not currently have.

**Alternative B — thread it explicitly.** Pass the diagnostics through each path. Cleanest typing, but replay has no load at finish time, so it would have to stash them somewhere anyway — the same cache with a different name.

I went with the cache because it is the only one of the three with no new I/O and no new plumbing through the replay engine, and because the value is derived, so a wrong answer can only produce a lock, never a divergent write. Say the word if you would rather have A.

add.issue.name: stop writing the user name into the event log file name

edit.description.md:
Write `<userId>.jsonl` instead of `<userId>.<userName>.jsonl`. Keep reading both — existing files keep their name segment and it is simply ignored.

## Why

- **`tombstone.contributor` cannot currently do what it claims.** It clears the display name from the registry, but the name is baked into a git-tracked file name, in history, permanently. Dropping the segment means future events carry no name on disk at all.
- One file per contributor forever, instead of one per name they have ever used. A rename currently starts a new log file.
- `sanitizeFilePart` stops being semantically load-bearing and becomes what its docstring already claims: a storage encoding.

## Sequencing — do NOT ship this in the same release as b48b746

The reader half (ignore the name segment, resolve names from the registry) shipped in b48b746. This ticket is the writer half and must land in a **later** release, once clients are on that one.

A pre-b48b746 client reading `<ulid>.jsonl` parses `userName` as `'unknown'` (the file name schema's default for a missing segment). `preferBestName('Alice', 'unknown')` then re-encodes `'Alice'` to `'alice'`, mismatches, and picks the log's — so Alice displays as "unknown".

That leaks into name *matching*, not just display. In the old `addIssueAssignee`, assigning "Alice" by name finds no candidate; with `createUnlinked` — which the failure message explicitly suggests — it mints a fresh ULID and writes a `create.contributor` for a second "Alice". A duplicate identity, persisted as a real event. This is the failure `mergeRegistryNames` carries a comment warning about.

It is also asymmetric: each contributor writes their own log file, so one person upgrading degrades everyone else's view of *that person*.

## The change

- `getPersistFileName` -> `${sanitizeFilePart(userId)}.jsonl`. `stageStateBranchOwnEventFile` follows it; the `.jsonl`-doubling guard in `getEventLogPath` still holds.
- No migration needed: `parseEventFileActor` splits on the first `.` and already falls through to the `'unknown'` default when there is no separator, so it reads both forms today.
- Close a sharp edge at the same time: `findEventLogAuthor` would return `name: 'unknown'` for an id in the log but absent from the registry, and its caller writes that straight into a `create.contributor`. It should refuse `'unknown'` rather than register somebody under it. Believed unreachable now that `ensureContributorCurrent` guarantees a record for every author, but worth closing rather than relying on that.

Deliberately a separate release — this ticket is the reader half, that one is the writer half, and shipping both at once mints duplicate contributors on pre-b48b746 clients. Sequencing and the hazard are recorded there.

add.issue.name: stop treating every materialization failure as fatal

edit.description.md:
`bootStateFromEventLog` fails the whole boot if any event fails to materialize:

```ts
const failures = results.filter(isFail);
if (failures.length > 0) return failed(`Materializing failed:\n...`);
```

The materializers are partial, not total — roughly 30 `materializeFail` sites, most of them preconditions ("Unable to locate node X", "Cannot edit readonly node", "missing contributor", "missing target"). Skipping an event, which is exactly what an unknown action or a concurrent edit causes, is what makes those preconditions untrue.

So a merge can produce a log that does not boot. Worse, it inverts who pays: the client that skipped the event is fine, while the client that understands *both* events is the one that cannot open the board. And it is permanent, because the log is append-only.

Demonstrated: `tombstone.contributor c1` followed by `rename.contributor c1` returns
`Materializing failed: rename contributor failed, cannot rename a removed contributor`.

## The split

- **Convergence failures** — ordering and preconditions. The event lost a race, or refers to state this replay does not have. Skip it and keep going; tombstone-wins and delete-wins fall out naturally.
- **Corruption failures** — invalid user id, malformed rank, bad payload. The log is genuinely broken. Still fatal.

Both currently go through the same `materializeFail`, so the distinction does not exist anywhere. Work is: give it a category, triage every site (each needs a real decision — no-op, or which side wins), and make boot fatal only on the corruption class.

## Consequences

- Silent divergence becomes possible: two clients can hold different state with nothing saying so. Needs to be visible — a count of events that could not be applied, surfaced rather than swallowed.
- Once replay is total, the board-wide unreadable lock is no longer load-bearing for ordering, and `RETIRED_EVENT_ACTIONS` goes away with it. Remove those two **together and last** — deleting the retired list before this work re-locks boards that carry an abandoned action.

add.issue.name: never auto-commit in the user's repo — only the state branch

edit.description.md:
Autosync creates commits in the user's own repository. Observed twice in one session on this repo: a commit titled "Initial commit" appeared unbidden, the second time capturing 17 staged files of unrelated work.

epiq owns the state branch worktree. It has no business writing commits in a repo that may hold unrelated or confidential work in progress. The exposure is not "a stray commit", it is arbitrary staged content captured into a commit nobody wrote.

## Chain

`startGuiAutoSync` runs `sync()` on a timer (15s here) -> `sync.ts:245` calls `ensureInitialCommit(repoRoot)` — the user's repo, not the state worktree -> guard misfires -> `git commit --allow-empty -m 'Initial commit'` with **no pathspec**, sweeping in whatever is staged.

Verified NOT affected: pushing. `pushStateBranch` always runs with `cwd: stateBranchRoot`, so only `__epiq_state__` is pushed and the stray commits stayed local.

## Three defects

1. **Reachable from sync at all.** `ensureInitialCommit` belongs on the `:init` path only, where the user explicitly asked to set the project up. It exists for a real reason — creating the state branch needs a commit to branch from — but that is a one-time, input-sourced bootstrap.
2. **Fails open.** `rev-parse --verify HEAD` exits non-zero for "no HEAD" *and* for "the command failed": a 10s timeout gives `exitCode: 124`, a spawn error or missing cwd gives `1`. Any of those currently reads as "empty repo". If we cannot positively confirm the repo has no commits, do nothing.
3. **Captures the index.** `--allow-empty` only permits an empty diff, it does not force one, so the commit takes whatever is staged. Use plumbing (`commit-tree` on the empty tree, then `update-ref`) so it is structurally incapable of committing user content.

(3) matters most: with plumbing, a future caller who gets the guard wrong still cannot take the user's files.

Consider also a shared assertion that no commit helper is invoked with `cwd === repoRoot` outside init, so this cannot regress quietly.

Workaround until fixed: `autoSync: false`, or do not leave the GUI running with staged work.

add.issue.comment.md:
Solution: fixed, uncommitted pending review. All three defects plus a fourth found on the way.

1. **Out of sync.** `ensureInitialCommit` removed from `sync.ts` and moved into `initCommand`, before the state branch is created. Nothing on the autosync path writes to the user's repo any more.
2. **Fails closed.** Switched to `rev-parse --verify --quiet HEAD` and now requires the unmistakable signal — exit 1 with *empty stdout and stderr*. Verified against real git: an unborn HEAD gives exactly that, while a bad cwd gives exit 128 with output. Anything ambiguous returns a failure and writes nothing.
3. **Cannot capture the index.** The commit is built by plumbing — `hash-object -w -t tree /dev/null`, `commit-tree`, `update-ref HEAD` — which never reads the index. Confirmed by hand first: with `secret.txt` staged, the resulting commit held no files and the file was still staged afterwards.
4. **Found while fixing:** `initCommand`'s own `[epiq:init-project]` commit had no pathspec either, so it swept staged work alongside `project.json`. Now pinned to `['.epiq/project.json', '.gitignore']`. `git.commit` gained an optional `pathspec`.

Message changed from `Initial commit` to `[epiq:init-repo]`, matching the other epiq-authored messages and making it obvious who wrote it.

## Tests — `source/test/git-safety.test.ts`, 14 of them

Real repositories under `os.tmpdir()`, each with its own `.git`, plus a harness assertion that refuses to run if the repo under test is not inside the temp dir — a test cannot retarget a real repository even by accident.

Behavioural: creates the bootstrap commit; the commit contains no files; **staged work stays staged and uncommitted** (the actual incident); untracked and modified files untouched; no-ops when commits already exist; no-ops without disturbing staged work; fails closed on an unreadable HEAD; writes nothing into a non-repo directory. Plus pathspec commits only the named paths, and the no-pathspec case documented so the hazard is visible.

Static guards against the whole class, not the instance: only `init.cmd.ts` may commit, stage, or push with `cwd: repoRoot`, and `sync.ts` must not mention `ensureInitialCommit`. Any new call site elsewhere fails the suite.

7 of the 14 verified red against the pre-fix code, including every one that matters.

Suite 570 pass, tsc + build:gui:types + prettier + eslint clean.

add.issue.name: Timeline is empty on first load until you touch a filter

edit.description.md:
The scrubber draws no bars and no dots on first load. Changing scope or a filter fills it in.

The socket URL embeds the board (`/ws?boardId=…`), so resolving the board tears down the socket and opens a new one. Two things then go wrong:

1. Child effects run before parent effects, so `TimeScrubber`'s `onRequestHistory` effect fires on the socket `App`'s effect is about to replace. Both replies die with it.
2. `replaced` suppresses `setConnected(false)`, so `connected` never flips across the swap and nothing re-requests history on the new socket.

`historyBuffer` publishes only when both halves land, so a lost `commits` reply leaves it pending forever — `historyId` stays 0 and `shown.timeline` stays null.

Traced with tagged sockets:

```
[sock] created 99648 boardId undefined
[ask] 1 on socket 99648
[recv] timeline 1 on socket 99648   <- commits reply never arrives
[ask] 2 on socket 99648             <- sent on the doomed socket
[sock] created 442 boardId 44MY70Q
[sock] closed 99648 replaced true
dots drawn: 0
```

Racy by nature: `timeline` answers in ~50ms and lands, `commits` takes ~950ms and misses the window, so it occasionally works. A failed half is also dropped silently — `if (nextCommits)` in `App.tsx` discards a `fail` Result with no retry.

Pre-existing, not from the hover-perf work: reproduces identically on unmodified `main`.

add.issue.name: Sync never retries a commit whose push failed

edit.description.md:
`sync.ts` gates the push on `if (createdCommit || bootstrapped)` — on this run having committed, not on the repo being ahead. There is no ahead/behind check anywhere; the only `@{u}` use is `hasUpstream`, an existence test.

So a commit whose push failed (offline, hook, rejection) is never retried until the user authors another event. Worse, the next run reports success: `pulled` is effectively always true, so `setSynced` says "Synced local state" while sitting ahead of the remote.

Fix: push when `git rev-list --count @{u}..HEAD > 0`, not when this run made a commit.

add.issue.name: An event written mid-sync fails the pull

edit.description.md:
`pullBranchRebaseIfPresent` runs a plain `git pull --rebase`, and nothing sets `rebase.autoStash`. Events are appended straight into the state-branch worktree and autosync runs on a timer, so a mutation landing between `git add` and the pull leaves the worktree dirty:

```
error: cannot pull with rebase: You have unstaged changes.
error: please commit or stash them.
```

Reproduced in a scratch repo. Self-heals next cycle, but surfaces as a spurious "Sync failed" and the window is open on every sync.

Fix: pass `-c rebase.autoStash=true` on the pull.

add.issue.name: isNonFastForward matches every push rejection

edit.description.md:
`isNonFastForward` returns true on `'failed to push some refs'`, which git emits for any rejection. Verified with a `pre-receive` hook that declines:

```
 ! [remote rejected] HEAD -> main (pre-receive hook declined)
error: failed to push some refs to '…'
```

That trips the retry path, which runs `pull --rebase` — rewriting state-branch history — before re-failing with the same hook error. A policy or permissions rejection should never cause a history rewrite.

Fix: match only `(non-fast-forward)` / `(fetch first)`, not the generic summary line.

add.issue.name: State-branch sync commit takes the whole index

edit.description.md:
`git.commit` documents that omitting `pathspec` "takes whatever the user happened to have staged", but `createStateBranchSyncCommit` goes through `commitAndGetSha`, which calls `git.commit({cwd, message})` with no pathspec.

The separate worktree makes this safer than in the user repo, but the guard is one-sided: `hasStagedChanges` inspects the whole index, so anything left staged there both triggers the commit and rides along in it.

Fix: commit the pathspec that was actually staged (own event file + media dir), and scope the staged-changes check to the same paths.

add.issue.name: Sync reports pulled/pushed when nothing moved

edit.description.md:
`pullBranchRebaseIfPresent` returns true whenever a remote branch exists and the pull ran — it means "attempted", not "received". `pushStateBranch` returns true on any exit-0 push, including *Everything up-to-date*.

Both feed the user-facing status text, which is how a stranded unpushed commit ends up labelled "Synced local state".

Fix: report what actually moved — compare HEAD across the pull, and detect an up-to-date push.

add.issue.name: Every pull does an ls-remote before its fetch

edit.description.md:
`hasRemoteBranch` shells out to `ls-remote` before every `fetch` in both the pull and reset paths, and returns `failed` on a non-zero exit. Two network round trips where one would do, and offline aborts at the remote-inspection step rather than after the local commit — so the error names the wrong thing.

Fix: fetch once and read the resulting remote-tracking ref locally.

`onPointerDown` dispatches a scrub and `endDrag` dispatches again on pointer up. With no movement between them both resolve to the same target time, so a single click asks the server to check out the same moment twice.

```
↑ time-travel:scrub    22:51:31.016
↓ time-travel:result   22:51:31.306
↓ state (83519)        22:51:31.310
↑ time-travel:scrub    22:51:32.831
↓ time-travel:result   22:51:33.136
↓ state (83519)        22:51:33.139
```

add.issue.name: Replay rebuilds logs and virtual fields once per event

edit.description.md:
Every scrub re-checks-out the board, and that was ~600ms on this repo. Measured at the socket and broken down:

```
load=20ms  reset=0.3ms  materialize=565-600ms   (1866-1917 events)
derive=1.5ms  slim=0.1ms  stringify=0.3ms  size=117KB
```

So the state broadcast is not the cost — serializing 117KB takes 0.3ms. `materializeAll` is 97% of it. Inside `completeMaterialization`, per event:

- `appendEventToAppLog` does `[...s.eventLog, event]` — copies the whole log every event, ~2M element copies over the replay. 177ms.
- `refreshAffectedVirtualNodes` rebuilds a ticket's six virtual field nodes once for every event that touches it, when only the final state is ever read. 310ms.

Both are quadratic in the log, the same shape as the derive that `materializeAll` already batches.

Fix: collect the app log, the per-node logs and the affected node ids during a replay and apply each once at the end. Nothing reads either log or the virtual nodes during materialization — only API-level code does — so the deferral is not observable.

Measured on this repo, 1992 events:

- `materializeAll` 662ms → 144ms
- scrub round trip at the socket ~600ms → ~150ms

Coverage was already there: `replay-equivalence.test.ts` deep-compares batched against per-event replay over a 300+ event log, which includes the node logs, the event log and the virtual nodes. add.issue.name: Scrub without re-materializing the board from scratch

edit.description.md:
Every scrub throws the board away and rebuilds it from event zero. After the per-replay batching in `3XACRX` a scrub is ~150ms on this repo (1992 events); the remaining cost is almost entirely `materializeAll`, and it grows with the log.

## Where it lives

`checkoutStateAt` in `source/mcp/epiq-time-travel.ts` does, per scrub:

1. `resolveStateBranchRoot`
2. `loadMergedEventsBefore(root, targetTime)` — reads and decodes **every** event file from disk, twice (applied + unapplied). ~20ms
3. `resetState()`
4. `materializeAll(appliedEvents)` — ~144ms
5. `patchState({readOnly: true, timeMode: 'peek', unappliedEvents, replay: null})`, then sets the module-level `currentAsOfTime`

The websocket handler (`source/gui/api/lib/websocket.ts`, `time-travel:scrub`) then calls `broadcastDerivedState()`.

**Do not spend time on the broadcast.** Measured: derive 1.5ms, slim 0.1ms, stringify 0.3ms for a 117KB payload. It is not the cost.

## Plan

**Step 1 — cache the decoded log.** Hold the decoded events in a module-level cache instead of re-reading and re-decoding per scrub. Key it on something that changes when the log does: the state branch HEAD sha (`git rev-parse HEAD` in the state worktree) plus the event dir mtimes, or invalidate explicitly from the sync path. Autosync writes events between scrubs, so a stale cache is the main hazard. Worth ~20ms and it is the prerequisite for step 2.

**Step 2 — step forward instead of resetting.** Keep the events already applied and the current `currentAsOfTime`. When the new target is *later*, apply only the events in `(currentAsOfTime, target]` with no `resetState()`. When it is *earlier*, fall back to the current reset-and-replay. Scrubbing drags in both directions, so this removes roughly half the work for free.

**Step 3 — only if steps 1–2 are not enough.** Periodic snapshots: deep-clone state every N events and replay from the nearest snapshot at or before the target, which also makes backward moves cheap. Measure the clone cost and memory before committing to it — this is the expensive option and may not be worth it.

## Constraints

- Nothing reads the event logs or ticket virtual nodes *during* materialization (only API-level code does), which is what made the `3XACRX` batching safe. Re-verify if you change what materialize does.
- `unappliedEvents` is patched into state and must stay correct on every path, including the forward-step one.
- Time travel is server-global and serialized by `runExclusive` in `epiq-time-travel.ts` — that lock is not re-entrant.
- `returnToLive` rebuilds via `materializeAll` and then `relockUnreadableEvents()`; any cache must be invalidated or reused correctly there too.

## Verification

`source/test/replay-equivalence.test.ts` is the right model and the existing guard for this area: it deep-compares a batched replay against a per-event one. Extend it so an incrementally-reached state at time T deep-equals a cold `checkoutStateAt(T)`, over a series of forward and backward targets including exact event boundaries. Confirm the new assertions actually fail when the incremental path is broken — the existing ones do.

Also run `npm run test:e2e` (docker, needs `npm run build:e2e:image`); it covers peek, replay and reboot, and is excluded from `npm test`.

## How to measure

In-process, against this repo: load events with `loadMergedEventsBefore`, `resetState()`, then time `materializeAll`.

End to end: start the GUI (`IS_LOCAL=true npx tsx source/Index.tsx gui`, read the port from its output — it falls back off 3710 if taken), connect a raw `ws` client, send `{type:'time-travel:scrub',payload:{targetTime}}` and time until `time-travel:result`. Discard the first scrub; it includes warm-up and reads ~1000ms against ~150ms steady state.

add.issue.name: Build ticket virtual fields only where they are read

edit.description.md:
A ticket's virtual field nodes (description, assignees, tags, comments, attachments, log) are built for every ticket a replay touches. After the per-replay batching in `3XACRX` they were still 112-128ms of the ~130ms `materializeAll` — 87% of what was left.

Nothing outside the TUI reads them. Consumers are `TicketUI`, `CommentListUI`, `AttachmentListUI`, `FieldListUI`, `command-validation` and `default-actions` / `edit.cmd` — all TUI. The GUI and MCP never touch them.

A process is either TUI or GUI (`Index.tsx` branches on `command === 'gui'`), and the MCP is its own entry, so a process-level switch is safe. They are derived state rebuilt from events on every boot and never persisted, so skipping them cannot affect what is written to disk.

Fix: `setVirtualNodesEnabled(false)` in `startGuiServer` and `source/mcp/index.ts`, gated in `refreshAffectedVirtualNodes`. Defaults on, so any path that does not opt out keeps today's behaviour.

Scrub round trip on this repo: ~150ms → 20-64ms.

Proof the GUI output is unchanged: captured the `state` payload for the same scrub target with the flag on and off — byte-identical.

Note the switch is set in `startGuiServer` rather than the `startGui` CLI wrapper, so the e2e-gui fixture (which calls the server directly) runs the same configuration the GUI ships with.

Also spotted: `materializeVirtualNodes` in `virtual-nodes.ts` has no callers and can go.

The chart keeps a previous scope's window while the buttons show the new one, and stays that way until the scope is changed again.

Seen with `Day` selected and the segment reading `23:50`. `segmentAt` only labels `HH:MM` for the minute unit, and `chooseSegmentUnit` only reaches minute below about two hours — at 24h it picks hour. So the axis was the `Hour` window while the controls said `Day`.

`TimeScrubber` decided which reply was its own by taking whichever history arrived next after a view change:

> A view change asks for one new window, so exactly the next history to arrive answers it.

That assumption does not hold. The gate opens during render, but the request is sent from a `useEffect` and `historyBuffer.open()` runs there — so between the two, a reply still in flight for the window just left can publish, close the gate with the wrong data, and leave the real reply ignored.

Fix: `requestBoardHistory` returns the id its reply will carry, and `TimeScrubber` accepts only that id. This removes `requestKey`, `steadyBoardId`, `heldKey`, `heldHistoryId`, `awaiting` and `seenHistoryId` — the machinery that existed to guess at what the id now settles.

Confirmed by manual testing. Not reproduced automatically: once the newer request calls `open()` the buffer drops the older reply, so the stale publish can only land in the short render-to-effect gap, which a test cannot steer into. `scrubber-scope.pw.ts` was added anyway and is labelled for what it is — it pins the invariant (whatever the buttons say, the axis is that scope) rather than guarding this race; it passes with and without the fix.

edit.description.md:
Write `<userId>.jsonl` instead of `<userId>.<userName>.jsonl`. Keep reading both — existing files keep their name segment and it is simply ignored.

## Why

- **`tombstone.contributor` cannot currently do what it claims.** It clears the display name from the registry, but the name is baked into a git-tracked file name, in history, permanently. Dropping the segment means future events carry no name on disk at all.
- One file per contributor forever, instead of one per name they have ever used. A rename currently starts a new log file.
- `sanitizeFilePart` stops being semantically load-bearing and becomes what its docstring already claims: a storage encoding.

## Sequencing — the gate is now open

The reader half (ignore the name segment, resolve names from the registry) shipped in b48b746, which went out in **v1.5.0**. This is the writer half, and it had to wait for a release that clients are actually on. That release exists now, so the only remaining condition is that the people sharing this board have upgraded to 1.5.0 or later.

The hazard this sequencing avoids, for the record: a pre-b48b746 client reading `<ulid>.jsonl` parses `userName` as `'unknown'` (the file name schema's default for a missing segment). `preferBestName('Alice', 'unknown')` then re-encodes `'Alice'` to `'alice'`, mismatches, and picks the log's — so Alice displays as "unknown".

That leaks into name *matching*, not just display. In the old `addIssueAssignee`, assigning "Alice" by name finds no candidate; with `createUnlinked` — which the failure message explicitly suggests — it mints a fresh ULID and writes a `create.contributor` for a second "Alice". A duplicate identity, persisted as a real event. This is the failure `mergeRegistryNames` carries a comment warning about.

It is also asymmetric: each contributor writes their own log file, so one person upgrading degrades everyone else's view of *that person*.

## The change

- `getPersistFileName` (`source/lib/event/event-persist.ts:140`) -> `${sanitizeFilePart(userId)}.jsonl`. `stageStateBranchOwnEventFile` follows it; the `.jsonl`-doubling guard in `getEventLogPath` still holds.
- No migration needed: `parseEventFileActor` splits on the first `.` and already falls through to the `'unknown'` default when there is no separator, so it reads both forms today.
- Close a sharp edge at the same time: `findEventLogAuthor` would return `name: 'unknown'` for an id in the log but absent from the registry, and its caller writes that straight into a `create.contributor`. It should refuse `'unknown'` rather than register somebody under it. Believed unreachable now that `ensureContributorCurrent` guarantees a record for every author, but worth closing rather than relying on that.

edit.description.md:
Every scrub throws the board away and rebuilds it from event zero. The cost grows with the log.

## Re-measure before doing anything

The numbers below were taken after `3XACRX` and before `PAM6JK2`, which landed straight after and disabled ticket virtual fields outside the TUI — 112–128ms of the ~130ms `materializeAll` those numbers attribute to it, in exactly the GUI process this ticket is about.

So the premise "the remaining cost is almost entirely `materializeAll`" is stale, and step 2 may now be optimising the wrong thing. Re-measure a GUI scrub first. If `materializeAll` has dropped to a few tens of ms, the ~20ms decode in step 1 is the dominant cost and step 1 alone may close this.

Numbers as they stood after `3XACRX` (1992 events): scrub ~150ms, of which `materializeAll` ~144ms.

## Where it lives

`checkoutStateAt` in `source/mcp/epiq-time-travel.ts` does, per scrub:

1. `resolveStateBranchRoot`
2. `loadMergedEventsBefore(root, targetTime)` — reads and decodes **every** event file from disk, twice (applied + unapplied). ~20ms
3. `resetState()`
4. `materializeAll(appliedEvents)`
5. `patchState({readOnly: true, timeMode: 'peek', unappliedEvents, replay: null})`, then sets the module-level `currentAsOfTime`

The websocket handler (`source/gui/api/lib/websocket.ts`, `time-travel:scrub`) then calls `broadcastDerivedState()`.

**Do not spend time on the broadcast.** Measured: derive 1.5ms, slim 0.1ms, stringify 0.3ms for a 117KB payload. It is not the cost.

## Plan

**Step 1 — cache the decoded log.** Hold the decoded events in a module-level cache instead of re-reading and re-decoding per scrub. Key it on something that changes when the log does: the state branch HEAD sha (`git rev-parse HEAD` in the state worktree) plus the event dir mtimes, or invalidate explicitly from the sync path. Autosync writes events between scrubs, so a stale cache is the main hazard. Likely the biggest remaining win now, and the prerequisite for step 2 either way.

**Step 2 — step forward instead of resetting.** Keep the events already applied and the current `currentAsOfTime`. When the new target is *later*, apply only the events in `(currentAsOfTime, target]` with no `resetState()`. When it is *earlier*, fall back to the current reset-and-replay. Scrubbing drags in both directions, so this removes roughly half the work for free. Value depends entirely on what the re-measure says `materializeAll` still costs.

**Step 3 — only if steps 1–2 are not enough.** Periodic snapshots: deep-clone state every N events and replay from the nearest snapshot at or before the target, which also makes backward moves cheap. Measure the clone cost and memory before committing to it — this is the expensive option and may not be worth it.

## Constraints

- Nothing reads the event logs or ticket virtual nodes *during* materialization (only API-level code does), which is what made the `3XACRX` batching safe. Re-verify if you change what materialize does.
- `unappliedEvents` is patched into state and must stay correct on every path, including the forward-step one.
- Time travel is server-global and serialized by `runExclusive` in `epiq-time-travel.ts` — that lock is not re-entrant.
- `returnToLive` rebuilds via `materializeAll`; any cache must be invalidated or reused correctly there too.

## Verification

`source/test/replay-equivalence.test.ts` is the right model and the existing guard for this area: it deep-compares a batched replay against a per-event one. Extend it so an incrementally-reached state at time T deep-equals a cold `checkoutStateAt(T)`, over a series of forward and backward targets including exact event boundaries. Confirm the new assertions actually fail when the incremental path is broken — the existing ones do.

Also run `npm run test:e2e` (docker, needs `npm run build:e2e:image`); it covers peek, replay and reboot, and is excluded from `npm test`.

## How to measure

In-process, against this repo: load events with `loadMergedEventsBefore`, `resetState()`, then time `materializeAll`. Note this path has virtual nodes **on**, unlike the GUI server — see `setVirtualNodesEnabled` — so it no longer reflects what a real scrub costs.

End to end, which does: start the GUI (`IS_LOCAL=true npx tsx source/Index.tsx gui`, read the port from its output — it falls back off 3710 if taken), connect a raw `ws` client, send `{type:'time-travel:scrub',payload:{targetTime}}` and time until `time-travel:result`. Discard the first scrub; it includes warm-up.

Description now leads with a re-measure step, and flags that the in-process measurement recipe no longer matches a real GUI scrub (virtual nodes are on in that path, off in the server). Also dropped the reference to `relockUnreadableEvents`, which `S1WEPQG` deleted.

add.issue.name: Pull fails with "Cannot rebase onto multiple branches" when FETCH_HEAD is written concurrently

edit.description.md:
Hit live during the v1.5.0 board sweep, on the first `epiq_sync` after a batch of MCP writes:

```
Failed during pull --rebase
git -c rebase.autoStash=true pull --rebase origin __epiq_state__
From https://github.com/ljtn/epiq
 * branch              __epiq_state__ -> FETCH_HEAD
fatal: Cannot rebase onto multiple branches.
```

An immediate retry succeeded, so it is a race, not a wedge.

`pullBranchRebaseIfPresent` runs `pull --rebase` with an explicit refspec. `pull` fetches into `FETCH_HEAD` and then rebases onto what it finds there. Git emits this exact fatal when `FETCH_HEAD` holds more than one mergeable entry — which is what a second fetch into the same worktree produces if it lands between our fetch and our rebase.

The state-branch worktree is shared: a running GUI's autosync, a TUI session and an MCP call all sync through it, on timers. So two `pull`s overlapping is the normal case, not an exotic one, and `FETCH_HEAD` is the shared mutable file they collide on.

Direction: stop depending on `FETCH_HEAD`. Fetch into the remote-tracking ref and rebase onto that by name (`git fetch origin __epiq_state__:refs/remotes/origin/__epiq_state__`, then `git rebase origin/__epiq_state__`) — a named ref is not clobbered by a concurrent fetch the way `FETCH_HEAD` is. `P4QTPMR` already moved the pull path toward reading the remote-tracking ref locally, so this follows the same line.

Serialising sync across processes would also close it, but that is a much bigger change than removing the `FETCH_HEAD` dependency.

Neighbours: `BZJR3VE` (a rebase that conflicts wedges sync permanently) and `55NWR3D` (the union merge driver that stops it conflicting). This one is upstream of both — the rebase here never started.

add.issue.name: boot() invents a project descriptor instead of reading the one on disk

edit.description.md:
`boot()` in `epiq-api.ts` attached the state worktree with:

```ts
const projectFileContents = getProjectFileContents();
await ensureStateBranchWorktree({..., stateBranchName: projectFileContents.stateBranch});
```

`getProjectFileContents()` does not read anything — it mints a fresh descriptor with a new ULID and `stateBranch: DEFAULT_STATE_BRANCH`. So every MCP and GUI operation assumed the state branch was `__epiq_state__` regardless of what `.epiq/project.json` says. It only ever worked because real projects use the default name.

Second, related gap: `boot()` attached a worktree without ensuring the local state branch exists, so a clone that has never synced failed with `fatal: invalid reference: <branch>`. That is the path a new collaborator takes.

Fix: resolve the branch with `getStateBranch(repoRoot)` and call `ensureLocalStateBranch` before `ensureStateBranchWorktree`.

Deliberately *not* the full `bootstrapStateBranchStorage` the sync path runs: that also runs `ensureStateBranchIsStorageOnly`, which commits a repair, and `boot()` is on every API call. Tried it first and it regressed `bulk.pw.ts` — verified by stashing the change and watching the test go green again.

Found by the collaboration harness (`source/test/e2e-collab`) on its first run, before it had ever passed.

add.issue.comment.md:
Solution: `pullBranchRebaseIfPresent` no longer uses `pull --rebase`. It fetches with an explicit refspec into `refs/remotes/origin/<branch>` and then rebases onto that ref by name, so nothing depends on `FETCH_HEAD`. Commit `KE8F9RY`.

`git.fetch` carries the explicit refspec, which also makes `ensureLocalStateBranch` independent of whether the remote's default fetch refspec is configured.

Reproduced deterministically first, in `source/test/e2e-collab/concurrent-sync.test.ts`: one actor runs three syncs at once against its single state worktree while another publishes between rounds. That is the GUI-autosync / TUI / MCP overlap the description names. Before the fix, with the exact reported error:

```
* branch            epiq/state -> FETCH_HEAD
  8644620..f779e12  epiq/state -> origin/epiq/state
fatal: Cannot rebase onto multiple branches.
```

The test also asserts the other actor's events still reach this one afterwards, so it fails on data loss as well as on the error string.

Green: 585 unit, 4 collab, 43 playwright, 11 docker e2e.

Followed the constraints in the description: it lives under `.epiq/` so `ensureStateBranchIsStorageOnly` does not remove it, and union is safe because line order is not load-bearing.

One thing the description did not anticipate: the sync commit is pathspec-scoped since `BB38JSS`, so the attributes file needed its own stage step (`stageStateBranchEventAttributes`) to be included. Staging alone was not enough.

```
hint: Resolve all conflicts manually…
```

add.issue.name: A test run rewrote the developer's branches and git identity

edit.description.md:
Running the suites from a git worktree located **inside** the main checkout (`.claude/worktrees/<name>`) corrupted the real repository:

- `main` was moved off `origin/main` onto a chain of test commits — `base`, `seed`, `initial`, `real work`, `no pathspec`, `test commit`, `[epiq:init-project]`
- `user.name=Test` / `user.email=test@example.com` were written into the shared `.git/config` at repo level, so every subsequent commit was misattributed
- a `MERGE_HEAD` containing `dummy` was left in `.git/worktrees/<name>/`, which blocks committing with `fatal: Corrupt MERGE_HEAD file`
- the worktree's HEAD was checked out onto `main`

Every stray commit message belongs to `git-safety.test.ts` — the suite whose stated purpose is that "epiq writes commits in the user's own repository in exactly one place".

## Not reproduced

Against a disposable clone (`git clone --no-local`), all of these were clean: `git-safety.test.ts` alone, the full unit suite, the collaboration suite, and the entire pre-push hook — run both in a normal checkout and in a worktree of it.

The one structural difference not yet tested: the worktree that got corrupted lived **inside** the parent repo's working tree, so a helper resolving a repo from `process.cwd()` can walk up into the parent, whose checked-out branch is `main`. That fits the evidence (commits landing on `main`, config written at repo level) but is unproven.

`makeRepo` in `git-safety.test.ts` guards correctly — mkdtemp, realpath, and a refusal to operate outside the temp dir — so the leak is likely a helper that takes a repo path from somewhere other than `makeRepo`.

## Mitigation already landed

The collaboration suite now runs in the e2e container with the checkout mounted **read-only** (`-v "$PWD":/app:ro`), so it cannot reach the host repository at all. The same treatment is worth extending to any suite that shells out to git.

## Still worth doing

Find the actual leak. A candidate check: assert in a global test setup that `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` from any repo a test operates on resolves under `os.tmpdir()`, and fail loudly otherwise — the guarantee `git-safety.test.ts` already claims, enforced for every suite rather than one file.

A `git push` rewrote the developer's branches and git identity:

- `main` was moved off `origin/main` onto a chain of test commits — `base`, `seed`, `initial`, `real work`, `no pathspec`, `test commit`, `[epiq:init-project]`
- `user.name=Test` / `user.email=test@example.com` were written into the shared `.git/config`, so every later commit was misattributed
- a `MERGE_HEAD` containing `dummy` was left in the git dir, which blocks committing with `fatal: Corrupt MERGE_HEAD file`
- the worktree's HEAD was checked out onto `main`

## Cause

**Git exports `GIT_DIR` into the environment of its hooks.** It overrides repository discovery, so every `git` the suite ran under `git push` was aimed at the developer's repository regardless of `cwd`.

That is why `makeRepo` in `git-safety.test.ts` did not help: it validates the *path*, and `GIT_DIR` bypasses paths entirely. Running the suites — or even `sh .husky/pre-push` — by hand never reproduces it, because only a real `git push` sets the variable.

Reproduced in a disposable clone by setting `GIT_DIR` and changing nothing else, giving the same signature: a `Test`-authored commit on the checked-out branch plus the injected identity.

Not worktree-specific. A plain checkout is equally exposed.

## Three paths were affected

1. Anything vitest runs.
2. The collaboration suite, which shells out to git heavily.
3. Playwright's `global-setup`, which spawns the GUI server on the host; it seeds by driving a real TUI, which inherited the variable.

add.issue.comment.md:
Correction to what this ticket first said: the original guess — that it was specific to a worktree living inside the parent checkout, letting a helper walk up into it — was wrong. The description now carries the real cause, `GIT_DIR`.

The reason that guess survived so long is worth recording: every attempt to reproduce it ran the suites, or `sh .husky/pre-push`, **by hand**. Only a real `git push` sets `GIT_DIR`, so the corrupting condition was never present in any of those runs. Four clean reproductions in a disposable clone all proved nothing.

Solution, in three commits:

- `source/test/setup/no-git-outside-tmp.ts` strips the variables for anything vitest runs, refuses to hand one to a child process, and fails a test that aims git at the checkout rather than a temp directory. Wired in via `setupFiles`.
- The collaboration suite runs in the e2e container with the checkout mounted read-only, so it cannot reach the host repository whether or not the cause is understood.
- Playwright's `global-setup` strips them before spawning the GUI server, which seeds by driving a real TUI. This one is invisible to the vitest guard and was the last failure standing.

The variable list is shared in `source/test/setup/git-hook-env.ts` rather than duplicated.

Verification:

- 591 unit tests pass under a real `git push` with `GIT_DIR` set; the same run previously failed 22 and corrupted the repo.
- Replaying the corrupting scenario with the fix: 14/14 pass, HEAD unchanged, no new damage.
- After a clean push: `main` still at `origin/main`, identity intact, no local overrides.
- Four tests cover the guard itself, so it cannot rot into decoration.

Left undone: `git-safety.test.ts` asserts "no commit reaches the user repository outside init" by scanning source for `cwd: repoRoot`. That is a static check and would not have caught this, since the escape needs no suspicious argument. Worth extending it to assert the environment is clean too.

add.issue.name: Internal state-branch git commit/push run the repo's own hooks and fail

edit.description.md:
`epiq_sync` never reaches the remote. `.epiq/log/epiq.log` shows every push failing:

```
[pushStateBranch]:failed Failed during state branch push
npm error Missing script: "lint:err"
```

Cause: `core.hooksPath` is repo-wide (an absolute path, so it applies to every worktree of this repo, including the internal state-branch storage worktree at `~/.epiq-global/worktrees/<projectId>`). `git.commit`/`git.push` in `source/git/git-commands.ts` don't pass `--no-verify`, so this repo's `.husky/pre-push` (lint/build/test/e2e/collab/gui) runs against that worktree on every sync push. That worktree only ever holds `.epiq/` — no `package.json` — so `npm run lint:err` walks up and finds an unrelated `~/package.json`, which lacks the script, and fails immediately. Every push (and, in a repo with a pre-commit hook, every commit) is blocked this way — not just here, in any project epiq is used in.

Fix: `git.commit` and `git.push` are only ever used for epiq's own bookkeeping (state-branch commits/push, `.epiq/project.json` init commit) — never the user's application changes — so they should always run with `--no-verify`.

add.issue.name: Give each Playwright worker its own GUI server so the suite can run parallel

edit.description.md:
The GUI suite is the largest part of the push gate: ~191s of it, more than the unit, e2e and collab suites combined. It runs at `workers: 1` because every worker would share one server over one repo.

Measured: `--workers=4` takes 105s instead of 191s, but 7 tests fail — issue-history, move, scrubber, tab-persistence. All of them mutate board state, so this is shared-state contention, not a timing flake.

## Why it is serial today

`playwright.config.ts` sets `workers: 1` and `fullyParallel: false`. `source/test/e2e-gui/global-setup.ts` spawns one `serve.ts`, which seeds one project (`seedProject()` in `seed-tui.ts`) plus one bare repo, and writes both URLs to a fixed path: `os.tmpdir()/epiq-gui-e2e-handoff.json` (`handoff.ts`). Every worker reads that one file, so every worker drives the same board.

## Steps

1. Replace the global-setup + handoff-file pair with a **worker-scoped Playwright fixture** (`test.extend({...}, {scope: 'worker'})`). A worker fixture runs inside the worker process, so it can hold `baseUrl`/`repoRoot` in memory and the handoff file can go away entirely.
2. Per worker: seed a project, start a `startGuiServer` on port 0, and tear both down in the fixture's cleanup.
3. Seeding drives a real TUI and is not cheap, so seeding once into a template directory and copying it per worker is likely faster than seeding N times. Measure before choosing.
4. Set `workers` to a number (4 is the measured point) and `fullyParallel: true`.
5. Confirm the 7 named tests pass, then re-measure. Anything near 105s is the win.

## Watch out

- `global-setup.ts` calls `stripGitHookEnv()` because under `git push` this runs from a hook with `GIT_DIR` exported, which would aim git at the developer's repository. Whatever replaces it must keep doing that — see `source/test/setup/git-hook-env.ts`.
- The bare-repo server (the "nothing to load here" screen) needs the same per-worker treatment.

Follow-on from FV6VS2M, which covered the unit and container suites.

Also documented `.epiq/log/epiq.log` in the readme. Regression test in `source/test/git-commands.test.ts` (real rejecting pre-commit/pre-push hooks). Merged in #108.

add.issue.name: Keep the format check out of worktrees checked out inside the repo

edit.description.md:
`npm test` runs `prettier --check "**/*.{ts,tsx}"`, and that glob walks into `.claude/worktrees/`. Another session's working copy fails the check, so the gate fails on code that is not on the branch being tested.

Same hole as the vitest one fixed in #107, which added `.claude/**` to the vitest exclude. Prettier was missed, and the repo had no `.prettierignore` at all.

Fix: add `.prettierignore` with `.claude/`.

Note: prettier resolves ignore patterns relative to the ignore file's own directory, so this only works at the repo root.

add.issue.name: Pin colour off for the test run so the suite does not depend on the terminal

edit.description.md:
`command-validation.test.ts` compares rendered strings against plain text, but chalk decides for itself whether to emit escape codes. A terminal that exports `FORCE_COLOR` (Ghostty and the Claude Code harness both do — `FORCE_COLOR=3`) makes 11 of those tests fail:

```
expected '[2m<ENTER> to confirm[22m' to be '<ENTER> to confirm'
```

The suite passes in a plain shell and fails in one of those terminals, so the pre-push gate rejects pushes that are perfectly good. Pre-existing — reproduces at cd2946f0, before #108 and #109.

Fix: `env: {FORCE_COLOR: '0'}` in `vitest.config.ts`, so the assertions do not depend on ambient colour detection.

Worth knowing: `FORCE_COLOR=0` on the command line masks this, which is how it went unnoticed while measuring test timings.

edit.description.md:
From the code review of PR #112 (branch pr/commit-diff-viewer).

`DiffPanel.tsx` hardcodes a single theme (`github-dark`) and this app only ever needs a handful of languages, but `@pierre/diffs` pulls in Shiki's entire bundled language-grammar and theme set. 12G0CG9 already fixed the *eager-load* cost (code-splitting so main.js dropped from ~12.5mb to 2.6mb, everything else lazy) — this is the remaining cost: every SEA binary still embeds ~400 files / ~14MB of grammars and themes nobody renders (COBOL, VHDL, Fortran, dozens of unused color themes), inflating build output and binary size.

add.issue.name: DiffPanel can't distinguish a newly-added empty file from an unchanged one

edit.description.md:
From the code review of PR #112 (branch pr/commit-diff-viewer).

`toDiffFileInput` in `DiffPanel.tsx` treats `before === ''` or `after === ''` as "did not exist at this revision" (add/delete), matching the server's existing missing-blob convention. When *both* are empty — a commit that adds a genuinely empty file — neither guard fires, so `MultiFileDiff` renders it as a no-op unchanged file instead of an addition, even though the commit's file list correctly shows it as changed.

Low impact (empty-file additions are rare, and there's no content to diff either way), so left as-is in #112. A real fix needs the change type (add/delete/modify) threaded through from `git diff --name-status` rather than inferred from empty strings — `getChangedFilePaths`/`CommitDiffFile` would need to carry it.

add.issue.name: Plan: diff/patch coverage indicator in the Commits tab

edit.description.md:
Design/investigation ticket, out of scope for the current Commits tab UX pass (X4CC7TG) — not to be built yet, just scoped.

## Idea
User: could we show code coverage in the Commits tab, e.g. a yellow segment alongside the existing green/red insertions/deletions bar? Discussed live — landed on **diff coverage**, not aggregate file coverage: of the lines a commit actually changed, what fraction are exercised by tests (same idea as Codecov's "patch coverage"). Scoped **per file inside the expanded diff**, not as a second bar on the collapsed commit row — coverage is a file/line property, an aggregate per-commit number wouldn't mean much when only some lines changed.

## The real constraint
Epiq works across arbitrary repos/languages. There is no realistic way to hand-roll coverage generation ourselves — that means invoking the right test runner for whatever language/framework a given repo uses, which is fragile and heavy scope creep for a git tool. The practical path is **bring-your-own-report**: read a coverage report the user's own toolchain already produces, entirely opt-in — no report found means no coverage segment shown, nothing enforced.

## Open questions (need a decision before building)
- **Format**: lcov (`.info`) is the closest thing to a universal format — emitted directly or convertible-to by most JS (istanbul/nyc/vitest), Python (coverage.py), Ruby (simplecov), Go (via gcov2lcov), etc. Worth supporting just lcov first, or more than one format?
- **Discovery**: how does epiq find the report — a fixed conventional path (e.g. `coverage/lcov.info`), a configurable path/glob in project settings, or both?
- **Staleness**: a coverage report is a snapshot; it goes stale the moment code changes after it was generated. Need some signal (report mtime vs. commit time?) so a stale report doesn't quietly mislead rather than just being absent.
- **Per-line data**: lcov gives per-line hit counts, so mapping "lines changed in this diff" ∩ "lines covered in the report" is mechanical once a report is parsed — the harder part is the three questions above, not the math.

Tag `human-input-needed` — format/config-surface choice affects every repo epiq points at, not just this one.

add.issue.name: Ticket switch with Commits tab open silently dropped the refetch

edit.description.md:
Found live while testing the Commits-tab performance work (9825TMR).

Switching directly from one ticket to another while the Commits tab was already open left the pane stuck on "Loading commits…" forever — only re-clicking the tab recovered it.

Root cause: two `useEffect`s in `App.tsx` both depend on state that changes on every ticket switch — the commits-fetch effect (keyed on `selectedIssue?.id`) and the websocket-creation effect (keyed on `[boardId, navigate, reconnectTick]`, where `navigate` from `useNavigate()` is not referentially stable). React runs cleanup functions for changed effects before running any of the new effect bodies, in declaration order. Since the socket effect is declared after the commits-fetch effect, a same-render change to both meant: socket-effect cleanup nulls `socketRef.current` → commits-fetch effect runs and calls `sendSocketJson(socketRef.current, ...)` against that now-null ref, which no-ops silently → socket-effect setup finally creates the new socket, too late for that request.

Fix: added a `navigateRef` (same pattern as the existing `selectedBoardIdRef`) so the socket effect no longer depends on `navigate`, and stopped tearing the connection down on every same-board navigation.

add.issue.name: Plan: select diff lines → comment or file a linked ticket

edit.description.md:
Design/planning ticket — not to be built yet. User request, verbatim intent below.

## The feature
In a diff view (DiffPanel and/or the Commits tab's expanded-commit diff — both render through `FileDiffView`), let the user click-and-drag across diff lines to select a range. The selection surfaces two actions, not just a bare "comment":
- **Comment**: adds a comment on the *current* ticket, quoting the selected file/line-range/code.
- **File ticket**: creates a *new* ticket whose description includes the code snippet plus the user's typed note, referencing the original ticket. The original ticket gets an automatic comment noting a new ticket was filed, referencing the new one back. Bidirectional link, both directions automatic.

User's own framing: "we already have ticket refs, so it could be enough" for the linking — i.e. a plain ref mention in text might be sufficient, no new relationship primitive required. Open below.

## Open questions (need a decision before building)
- **Where does selection live**: is line-range selection a capability of `FileDiffView` itself (so it works everywhere a diff renders), or scoped to just one of the two current diff surfaces first? Depends on what `@pierre/diffs`' `MultiFileDiff` exposes for line-level interaction — worth checking its API before assuming a custom selection overlay is needed.
- **Is a ref mention enough, or does this need real ticket linking?** A plain `<REF>` mention in the description/comment text (matching the existing commit↔ticket convention) is the cheap path and needs nothing new. The gap: nothing currently makes a ref mention *clickable* or queryable — no "linked tickets" list, no backlink index beyond full-text search. If the plain-text mention plus the two auto-comments (this ticket → "filed X" / new ticket → "filed from Y") reads as sufficient linking, no new primitive is needed. If not, ref-mentions-as-links is a separable, more broadly useful feature (would help commit refs too) worth its own ticket rather than being built as a one-off inside this feature. Leaning toward the plain-mention version, human-input-needed on committing to that.
- **Filing UI**: presumably a small modal (matching `CreateNodeModal`'s existing pattern) with a text field for the note, showing the attached snippet read-only. Snippet stored as a fenced code block (path + line range as a header line) in the new ticket's description, since descriptions already render markdown.
- **Where does the filed ticket land**: Backlog, matching normal ticket creation? Any default tag (e.g. reusing the `from-review` convention, or a new `from-code-comment`-style tag) to mark provenance?
- **Scope of "comment on current ticket"**: is this only available when a diff is being viewed *from* a ticket's Commits tab (so "current ticket" is unambiguous), or also from the scrubber-dot `DiffPanel` flow, which isn't opened from any one ticket?

Once these are settled, break into sub-tickets the way the Commits-tab UX pass (X4CC7TG) was.

No custom selection overlay needed — this is exactly the shape the library was built for.

Proceeding with the other open questions as already leaned in the description (plain ref-mention linking, modal-based filing UI, Backlog + a provenance tag, available from both diff surfaces) since the user asked to start building. Breaking into sub-tickets now.

General bug in `MarkdownContent`, surfaced by diff-selection comments but affecting every markdown surface (ticket descriptions too).

`code` decides block-vs-inline with `isBlock = Boolean(className)`, but react-markdown only sets `className` when the fence names a language.
