add.issue.name: getSortedEvents blows the stack at ~4.7k events — board becomes permanently unopenable

edit.description.md:
`visit()` in `getSortedEvents` (`source/lib/event/event-load.ts:~430`) recurses once per event. Every event refs its predecessor, so the causal forest is one long linked list and recursion depth == log length.

Measured (binary search, `getSortedEvents` on a synthetic chain): **largest surviving chain is 4686 events**. At 4687 it throws `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`.

Blast radius: total. The throw is uncaught inside `loadAllPersistedEvents`, so TUI, GUI and MCP all fail to open the board — for *every* client, permanently, because the log is append-only and already pushed. No malicious actor required: `epiq-time-travel.ts` notes this repo's own log is already ~1.2k events. Normal use reaches the ceiling.

Fix: make the traversal iterative (explicit stack). No behaviour change to the resulting order.

Regression test: a chain of 50k events must sort without throwing.

Found by adversarial stress testing on branch `worktree-security-stress-audit`.

add.issue.name: One unparseable log line takes the whole board offline for every client

edit.description.md:
`parsePersistedEventsFile` (`source/lib/event/event-load.ts`) returns `failed(...)` for the *entire file* when a single line fails `JSON.parse`, or when `parsePersistedEnvelope` rejects the envelope. `loadAllPersistedEvents` propagates that, so one bad line = no board, anywhere.

Confirmed both shapes:
- truncated line → `Failed to parse event JSON from <file>`
- `{"v":1,"id":"not-a-tuple",...}` → `Invalid persisted event envelope: id`

Why this is not hypothetical: the logs are `*.jsonl merge=union`. Union merge splices the two sides line-by-line; if a file ever lacks a trailing newline (interrupted write, full disk, killed process mid-`appendFileSync`) the merge concatenates two half-lines into one invalid one. That corrupt line is then committed and pushed, and every client that pulls it loses the board permanently — the log is append-only, so there is no in-band repair.

This contradicts the stated invariant "Unreadable stays ordered". That path exists (`UnreadableEvent`, `reportUnreadableEvents`) but only covers unsupported `v` and unknown actions — not a line this build cannot parse at all.

Fix: quarantine rather than abort. A line that will not parse should become an `UnreadableEvent` (reason `unparseable`), be reported through the existing channel, and leave the rest of the log loadable. Keep the bytes untouched.

Found by adversarial stress testing on branch `worktree-security-stress-audit`.

add.issue.name: A ULID at TIME_MAX in the log permanently bricks every write on every machine

edit.description.md:
`persist` (`source/lib/event/event-persist.ts`) seeds the next id from the edge:

```ts
getNextId(Math.max(Date.now(), decodeTime(edgeRef.value) + 1))
```

If any event in the log carries an id whose ULID timestamp is `TIME_MAX` (281474976710655), then `decodeTime(edge) + 1` exceeds what ULID can encode and `ulid` throws:

`Cannot encode a time larger than 281474976710655: 281474976710656 (ENC_TIME_SIZE_EXCEED)`

Confirmed in a probe. `persist` catches it, so nothing crashes — it just returns `failed` forever. The board goes permanently read-only for **every** client that pulls the log, and because the log is append-only there is no way back.

Cost to attack: one line in one's own event file. The id is chosen by the writer and nothing validates it on read.

Fix (both ends):
- On write: refuse to seed from an edge whose decoded time is implausible (e.g. more than a small window ahead of `Date.now()`); fall back to `Date.now()` and log it. A poisoned edge must not stop the board.
- On read: treat an event id whose timestamp is beyond a sanity bound as unreadable/quarantined rather than letting it become the edge.

See also the sibling ticket on far-future (but legal) timestamps.

Found by adversarial stress testing on branch `worktree-security-stress-audit`.

add.issue.name: Duplicate event ids make two machines derive different boards from the same event set

edit.description.md:
`getSortedEvents` dedupes by event id (`placed` set), but when two *different* events share one id it keeps whichever it visits first — and that is decided by `childrenByRef` insertion order, which follows `readdirSync` order over the event files.

Confirmed: the same three-event set fed in two orders produces two different sorted results (`edit.title → "AAA"` vs `edit.title → "BBB"`). Same event set, different board. That breaks the core contract: *same event set ⇒ same order ⇒ same board*.

Two ways in:
- Malicious: an actor deliberately reuses another actor's event id with a different payload, in their own log file. Nothing checks it.
- Accidental: any future code path that re-serialises a line with different key order defeats `merge=union` line identity and lands the same id twice.

Sibling sort is `a.id[0].localeCompare(b.id[0])`, which is 0 for equal ids, so `Array.sort` stability leaves file order in control.

Fix: make the tiebreak total. When two events share an id, order (and pick) them by a deterministic function of their full content — e.g. compare the canonical JSON of the line — so every machine keeps the same one. Optionally report the collision as an unreadable/conflicted event so it is visible rather than silent.

Found by adversarial stress testing on branch `worktree-security-stress-audit`.

add.issue.name: GUI WebSocket accepts cross-origin handshakes — any website can drive the whole board

edit.description.md:
`setupWebsocket` (`source/gui/api/lib/websocket.ts`) constructs `new WebSocketServer({server, path: '/ws'})` with no `verifyClient` and no Origin check anywhere in `source/gui`.

WebSockets are exempt from the same-origin policy, so any page the user visits while the GUI is running can open `ws://127.0.0.1:3710/ws` and send whatever it likes. The port is the fixed preferred port 3710, so it needs no guessing.

Confirmed live against a real `startGuiServer`: handshake accepted with `Origin: https://evil.example`, and the server dispatched our frames — `state:get` returned board state, `swimlane:create` reached the mutation path.

What a hostile page gets: the entire message surface. `issues:create`, `swimlane:create`/`delete`/`move`, `issue:close`/`reopen`, `issue:edit:title`/`description`, `issue:comment:add`/`delete`, `contributor:remove`, `issues:move` — plus `sync`, which runs `git push` to the shared remote, `time-travel:scrub`, which puts the board read-only, and `commit:inspect`, which writes a temp file and spawns the user's editor.

So a drive-by page can silently corrupt or wipe the shared board for every collaborator and push the damage.

Fix: `verifyClient` (or an `upgrade` handler) that rejects any handshake whose `Origin` is not the loopback origin this server is serving. Reject rather than accept-then-ignore, so the client sees it.

Note `epiq.localhost` is the advertised URL, so the allowlist needs both `http://epiq.localhost:<port>` and `http://127.0.0.1:<port>`.

Found by adversarial stress testing on branch `worktree-security-stress-audit`.

add.issue.name: GUI HTTP mutations are CSRF-able — no Origin or content-type check on /api

edit.description.md:
`startGuiServer` (`source/gui/api/api-server.ts`) accepts `POST /api/comments` and `POST /api/attachments` without checking `Origin` or `Content-Type`.

A `POST` with `Content-Type: text/plain` is a CORS *simple request*: the browser sends it with no preflight, and the attacker never needs to read the response. So any page the user visits can write comments and attachments into the board.

Confirmed live: `POST /api/comments` with `Content-Type: text/plain;charset=UTF-8` and `Origin: https://evil.example` reached the handler (returned the handler's own 400 for a missing project, not a rejection).

`DELETE /api/comments/:id` and `DELETE /api/attachments/:id` are preflighted and so are protected by CORS today — but only incidentally, and only in a browser.

Fix: one guard in front of every non-GET `/api` route — require an `Origin` header matching this server's own loopback origin, and require `application/json`. Pairs with the WebSocket Origin ticket; both should land together or the hole stays open.

Found by adversarial stress testing on branch `worktree-security-stress-audit`.

add.issue.name: A forged root event reorders all of history in front of init.workspace

edit.description.md:
`getSortedEvents` treats every event with `refId === null` as a root and sorts roots against each other by ULID. Only the genesis event is meant to be a root, but nothing enforces that.

Confirmed: appending one line with `id: ["00000000000000000000000000", null]` makes that event sort first, ahead of the real `init.workspace`, for every client.

Consequences: replay order changes globally. Anything the forged root does runs against an uninitialized state (a `materializeSkip`, so not fatal), but the reordering itself is the problem — it shifts the whole derived history and any ordering-sensitive materialization behind it, and it is trivially cheap to do.

Related: `splitEventsAtTime` decides applied/unapplied from `decodeTime(eventId)`, so a low forged timestamp also lands the event in every historical checkout.

Fix options to weigh:
- Treat a second root as an orphan (anchor it after the known history) rather than as a peer of genesis.
- Or: pin genesis explicitly — the `init.workspace` event is the only legal root; other `refId: null` events sort as orphans.

Both keep the log untouched and stay a pure function of the event set.

Found by adversarial stress testing on branch `worktree-security-stress-audit`.

add.issue.name: A far-future ULID drags every later event id a century forward, permanently

edit.description.md:
Weaker sibling of the TIME_MAX brick, and it needs no illegal value at all.

`persist` seeds ids with `Math.max(Date.now(), decodeTime(edge) + 1)`. One event whose ULID timestamp is, say, 100 years out is perfectly legal ULID, so nothing rejects it — but from then on *every* event minted by *every* client inherits that lower bound.

Confirmed: with such an edge, the next minted id decodes to `2126-08-05`.

What breaks, for everyone, forever:
- `createdAt` on every subsequent node is a century out.
- The time scrubber / `getEventTimeline` bucket range spans 100 years, so the real history collapses into one pixel.
- `checkoutStateAt` / `splitEventsAtTime` cut by `decodeTime`, so time travel over recent history stops working.

This is causality doing exactly what it is supposed to (the logical clock must not go backwards), which is why the fix belongs on the *seed*, not on the ordering: cap how far ahead of wall clock an edge is allowed to push the next id, and report when it is clamped. Ordering must keep using `refId` + ULID as today.

Should be fixed alongside the TIME_MAX ticket — same code path, same guard.

Found by adversarial stress testing on branch `worktree-security-stress-audit`.

add.issue.name: No size cap on titles, descriptions, tag names or assignee names on any surface

edit.description.md:
Comments are the only text with a limit (`MAX_COMMENT_LENGTH = 4000`, enforced in `addIssueComment` and the TUI). Everything else is unbounded on every surface:

- MCP (`source/mcp/server.ts`): `title: z.string().min(1)`, `description: z.string()`, `tagNames: z.array(z.string())` — no `.max()` anywhere, and no cap on array length either.
- GUI WebSocket: payloads go straight through, no schema at all.
- GUI HTTP: `readJsonBody` caps the *request* at 1 MB, but nothing caps the field.

Every one of those is written into the append-only log and replicated to every clone forever. A 50 MB description is one call away, and there is no way to remove it afterwards. Confirmed a 50 MB single-event line parses and loads (~46 ms), so it is not a crash — it is permanent, unbounded, irreversible bloat, and the same is available to any hostile page via the unauthenticated WebSocket.

Fix: one shared limits module next to `comment.limits.ts` with caps for title, description, tag name, assignee name and tag/assignee array length. Enforce in the `epiq-api` functions (the single gate both transports pass through, the way `addIssueComment` already does), and mirror the caps into the MCP zod schemas so the client gets told before the call.

Found by adversarial stress testing on branch `worktree-security-stress-audit`.

add.issue.name: createIssue is the only title path that skips sanitizeInlineText

edit.description.md:
Every other title write runs the input through `sanitizeInlineText` first — `createSwimlane` (`epiq-api.ts:727`), `editSwimlaneTitle` (:781), `editIssueTitle` (:1197), and even the tag and assignee names inside `createIssue` itself (:466, :495).

`createIssue` passes `input.title` straight to `createIssueEvents` unsanitized, so control characters, newlines, tabs and runs of whitespace land in the log verbatim.

Consequences: a title with `\n` or ANSI-adjacent control bytes breaks TUI row rendering and the GUI card layout, and it is permanent — the log is append-only, and `editIssueTitle` would sanitize a *replacement* but the original event stays in history and in every replay/time-travel view.

Fix: sanitize (and trim, and reject if empty after) in `createIssue`, matching the other three. Add a test asserting all four title entry points agree.

Found by adversarial stress testing on branch `worktree-security-stress-audit`.

add.issue.name: WebSocket message payloads reach the API unvalidated

edit.description.md:
`setupWebsocket` does `JSON.parse(raw) as GuiMessage` and then trusts the cast. `GuiMessage` is a compile-time type only; there is no runtime schema, so every handler spreads attacker-controlled shapes straight into `epiq-api`:

```ts
const result = await addIssueComment({repoRoot, ...message.payload});
```

The MCP surface does this properly with zod per tool. The WebSocket — the *less* trusted of the two, since it is reachable cross-origin today — does none of it.

Observed against a live server:
- `{"type":"issue:close"}` → `error: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'issueId')` — an internal TypeError echoed to the client.
- `null` → `error: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'type')`.
- `{"type":"time-travel:scrub","payload":{"targetTime":"NaN"}}` and `-1e308` are accepted and passed into `checkoutStateAt` / `splitEventsAtTime`.

Nothing crashed the server (good), but "does not crash" is not the bar — extra/unknown keys in a payload are spread into API inputs, and a wrong-typed field reaches git and state code that assumed the type.

Fix: a zod discriminated union over `GuiMessage`, parsed once at the top of the message handler, replacing the cast. Reject unparseable frames with a plain error and never spread a raw payload. Numeric fields (`targetTime`, `start`, `end`) need finite-number bounds, not just `z.number()`.

Found by adversarial stress testing on branch `worktree-security-stress-audit`.

add.issue.name: Make the multi-client e2e collab suite adversarial, not just concurrent

edit.description.md:
`source/test/e2e-collab/` proves well-behaved actors converge. It does not prove the system survives a badly-behaved or unlucky one, which is where every prio-1 finding in this batch lives — each was found by a one-file probe, not by the suite.

Cases the suite should gain, all driven through the existing multi-machine harness so they exercise real git sync:

**Malformed / hostile log content** (write the line directly into an actor's own log file, then sync):
- a truncated last line with no trailing newline, so union merge concatenates it with the other side's first line
- a line that is valid JSON but an invalid envelope
- an event id reused from another actor with a different payload — assert both machines derive the *same* board
- a second `refId: null` root with a low ULID
- an event id at ULID TIME_MAX, and one 100 years out — assert the board still accepts writes afterwards

**Scale**
- a log past the `getSortedEvents` recursion ceiling (>5k events) across several actors; assert every machine still opens the board and that batched replay still equals per-event replay at that size

**Concurrency**
- both actors syncing while one is mid-append (the `rebase.autoStash` path)
- a `sync` racing a `time-travel:scrub` on the same repo
- interrupted sync: kill the actor between commit and push, then sync again

Every case asserts the same two things the suite already asserts — identical event sets, identical derived order — plus "the board still opens" and "writes still work".

Depends on the prio-1 fixes: several of these will fail until they land, which is the point — land the test with the fix.

Found by adversarial stress testing on branch `worktree-security-stress-audit`.

add.issue.name: readJsonBody corrupts multi-byte UTF-8 across chunk boundaries

edit.description.md:
`readJsonBody` (`source/gui/api/api-server.ts`) accumulates with `body += chunk`, which decodes each `Buffer` chunk in isolation as UTF-8. A character whose bytes straddle two socket reads decodes to replacement characters on both sides.

Affects `POST /api/comments` and `POST /api/attachments` (the `name` field; `dataBase64` is ASCII and safe). Silent — the JSON still parses, the text is just wrong, and it is then written into the append-only log.

Fix: collect chunks into a `Buffer[]` and `Buffer.concat(...).toString('utf8')` once at `end`, or pipe through a `StringDecoder`. `readGitBlobsBatch` in `git-utils.ts` already documents exactly this hazard and handles it correctly — same treatment here.

Found by adversarial stress testing on branch `worktree-security-stress-audit`.

add.issue.name: mergePersistedEvents is unused code that violates every log invariant

edit.description.md:
`source/git/merge.ts` exports `mergePersistedEvents` / `serializePersistedEvents` / `writeFileIfChanged`. Nothing in `source/` calls them outside `source/test/merge.test.ts` — the real merge is git's `*.jsonl merge=union`.

As written they break three stated invariants at once:
- **Orders by wall clock.** `getEventTime` sorts on `decodeTime(event.id[0])`. The architecture rule is "never order, compare or resolve conflicts by wall clock".
- **Rewrites and reorders existing lines.** `serializePersistedEvents` re-emits the whole file via `JSON.stringify`. Byte identity per line is exactly what makes union merge safe; re-serialising can change it and produce duplicate lines on the next merge.
- **De-duplicates.** `byId.set(compositeKey, event)` silently drops one of two events sharing a key, last-writer-wins by array order.

It is also fully property-tested, which makes it read as supported API rather than as the hazard it is.

Decide and do one of:
- delete it (plus its test), or
- keep it behind a clear "recovery tooling only, never on the sync path" boundary and rewrite the ordering to use `refId` + ULID like `getSortedEvents` does.

Filing rather than deleting unilaterally — the test suite's investment suggests it was meant for something.

Found by adversarial stress testing on branch `worktree-security-stress-audit`.

add.issue.name: persist re-reads and re-sorts the entire log for every single event

edit.description.md:
`persist` calls `getEdgeRef(rootDir)`, which calls `loadAllPersistedEvents` — every event file read from disk, parsed, and run through `getSortedEvents` — just to take `.at(-1)`.

`materializeAndPersistAll` calls `persist` once per event, so an N-event log costs O(N) per write and O(N·M) for an M-event batch. `createIssue` with a description, three tags and two assignees is ~9 events, so ~9 full log reads per ticket.

Measured on a synthetic single-file log:

| events | ms per persist |
|---|---|
| 100 | 0.48 |
| 500 | 0.76 |
| 1000 | 1.34 |
| 2000 | 2.63 |
| 4000 | 4.98 |

Linear, ~1.25 µs/event, so ~45 ms of pure re-reading for one `createIssue` at 4k events. Not urgent today — the `getSortedEvents` recursion ceiling caps the log at ~4.7k anyway — but it becomes the next wall as soon as that ceiling is lifted, so it belongs in the same area of work.

Fix: resolve the edge once per batch in `materializeAndPersistAll` and thread it through, advancing it locally per event rather than re-reading. Must stay correct under a concurrent writer appending to another actor's file mid-batch — that is exactly what the re-read was buying, so the change needs a collab test.

Found by adversarial stress testing on branch `worktree-security-stress-audit`.

add.issue.name: getBootNavigationTarget throws instead of returning a Result
A display name containing ".jsonl" locks the user out of writing entirely

edit.description.md:
`getEventLogPath` (`source/lib/event/event-persist.ts`) guards the composed file name with:

```ts
/^(?!.*\.jsonl.*\.jsonl).*\.jsonl$/
```

`sanitizeFilePart` keeps `.` (a name like "J. Lampa" is meant to survive as `j.-lampa`), so a user whose display name contains the literal `.jsonl` produces `<id>.a.jsonl.b.jsonl`, the guard rejects it, and `persist` fails for every event that user ever writes. The board simply refuses their writes with `Invalid event log file name`.

Narrow, but it is a permanent self-inflicted lockout with a confusing message, and the fix is cheap.

Fix: sanitize the name segment so it cannot contain `.jsonl` (e.g. collapse the sequence during `sanitizeFilePart`) rather than rejecting the composed path after the fact. The guard can stay as a belt-and-braces assertion.

Found by adversarial stress testing on branch `worktree-security-stress-audit`.

add.issue.name: Decide the trust model: any writer can forge events as any contributor

edit.description.md:
Not a bug — a design boundary that should be written down deliberately rather than inherited.

Actor identity comes from the log **file name** (`parseEventFileActor`), and `stripActor` keeps it out of the payload on purpose. So anyone who can push to the state branch can create `.epiq/events/<victim-ulid>.<victim-name>.jsonl` and every event in it is attributed to that person, on every client, forever. There are no signatures and nothing cross-checks the file name against anything.

That is a coherent position for a git-based tracker — push access is the trust boundary, same as it is for the code — but it means the board's audit trail (who closed this, who removed that contributor, whose `Solution:` comment this is) is only as trustworthy as the weakest push credential, and the docs do not say so.

Options:
1. **Document and accept.** Add it to the architecture skill as an explicit non-goal: "attribution is advisory; push access is the trust boundary." Zero code.
2. **Sign the log.** Each actor signs their own file (or git-signs their commits) and clients mark unverified attribution. Real work, real key-management story, and it changes what "same event set ⇒ same board" means when signatures fail to verify.
3. **Middle ground.** Cross-check that an event file's commits were authored by the matching git identity, and surface a mismatch in the GUI rather than rejecting it.

Blast radius reaches ordering and replay, so this is yours to call rather than mine.

Raised by adversarial stress testing on branch `worktree-security-stress-audit`.

add.issue.comment.md:
Solution: 5547eca8, merged in PR #115. New `CodeSnippet` component wrapping `@pierre/diffs`' `File` — same shiki highlighter and `github-dark` theme as the diff view, language inferred from the marker's `filePath`, with the file header and line numbers disabled (the caption above already names the file and range, and the snippet's own numbers would start at 1 rather than at the real lines).

The comment body still stores the snippet as an ordinary fenced block, so it stays readable in any markdown-only renderer; `extractCommentSnippet`/`stripCommentSnippet` pull it back out at render time. Verified live: TypeScript tokenization (keywords, strings, template-literal interpolations) matches the diff view exactly.

add.issue.comment.md:
Solution: 44276b81, merged in PR #115. Block-ness now comes from a React context set by the `pre` renderer — i.e. from actually being inside the `<pre>` react-markdown wraps fenced blocks in — rather than from `Boolean(className)`, which is only set when the fence names a language. add.issue.name: Decide how agents are tracked on the board: own identity, extra assignee, or tag

edit.description.md:
Every ticket is assigned to the same human because `getActor` (`source/mcp/epiq-api.ts:271`) reads the one global `~/.epiq/config.json` for every MCP session. So N concurrent agents are one contributor, `self:true` always means the human, and the board can't say which agent is on what.

Options:

1. **Give each agent its own contributor identity.** Let the MCP actor come from the environment (`EPIQ_USER_ID`/`EPIQ_USER_NAME`) before falling back to config; each agent session exports its own. Attribution then falls out of the existing machinery: the agent writes its own `<ulid>.jsonl`, so `parseEventFileActor` attributes every move/comment/close to it, retroactively, in the scrubber and in `hasAuthoredEvents`. `self:true` assigns the agent, so the epiq skill rule needs no change. Assignees are already an array, so the human stays on the ticket alongside. Optionally link agent -> human with the existing `link.contributor.user`.
2. **Convention only, no code.** Agents add themselves as a second assignee via `createUnlinked`. Works today, but the log still says the human did it, and `↗` then means both "external human" and "agent".
3. **Tag per agent.** Cheapest, but tags are topical, they don't roll up, and they answer a question the contributor registry exists to answer.
4. **New ticket prop `agent`.** New event type, materializer, filter, GUI and TUI. A third answer to "who", empty for all history.

Trade-offs and couplings:
- Costs of 1: more identities means more log files, which pulls in ZFZFW9D (drop the name segment) — do that first. Names must be stable and few (`claude`, not one ULID per session) or the registry fills with noise.
- An env-set actor is a claim, not an authentication — same boundary as FV86AFC. Decide there whether agent attribution is meant to be trustworthy or advisory.
- A `kind: 'human' | 'agent'` flag on `Contributor` is worth having under either 1 or 2, so an agent renders as an agent rather than reusing the external marker.

add.issue.name: Make a diff comment's file/line reference a link back into the diff

edit.description.md:
A diff-selection comment names its file and line range, but that caption is inert — you have to find your way back to the diff by hand.

Make it a link that opens the Commits tab with the right commit expanded, the right file expanded, and the commented lines selected/scrolled into view.

Needs router work: the deep link has to survive a reload and be shareable, so the location goes in the URL as search params alongside the existing `tab=code` (commit sha, file path, line range, side) rather than being held in transient state.

The marker metadata currently carries `filePath` and the range but **not the commit sha** — a file can appear in several of a ticket's commits, so the sha has to be added for the link to be unambiguous. Keep it optional when parsing so comments written before this change still render their inline annotation; they just won't be clickable.

add.issue.name: Resolve the actor from the environment so agents write as themselves

edit.description.md:
Option 1 from 01M173SZ, decided. `loadSettingsFromConfig` is the single funnel every surface reads its identity through (TUI boot, GUI init, MCP `getActor`), so the override goes there.

- `EPIQ_USER_NAME` set: that name is the actor. `EPIQ_USER_ID` optionally pins the id; when it is absent the id is **derived deterministically from the name**, so one agent name is one identity forever, on every machine. That is what keeps the identity count bounded and the log file count small — a per-session random ULID would mint a new contributor and a new log file per run.
- The name matching the configured user is a no-op, so an agent cannot accidentally fork the human's identity.
- A malformed `EPIQ_USER_ID` fails the load rather than falling back to config — a silent fallback means the agent writes as the human, which is the bug being fixed.
- Nothing is written back to `config.json`; the override is process-scoped.

`ensureContributorCurrent` already registers any unknown author on its first write, so the agent appears in the registry with no extra work.

Follow-up, not in scope here: an env name equal to an *existing* contributor's name still derives a different id and creates a second record under that name.

add.issue.name: Board stops loading at ~9k events: getSortedEvents recurses once per event

edit.description.md:
`visit` in `getSortedEvents` (`source/lib/event/event-load.ts:437`) recurses into each child, and every event's `refId` is the previous edge, so the causal forest is one near-linear chain and the recursion depth is the event count. Past the V8 stack it throws `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`, which is not a `Result` — it escapes `loadAllPersistedEvents` and kills the process rather than failing the load.

Measured on a synthetic linear log (node 24, default stack):

| events | result |
| --- | --- |
| 7 000 | loads, 10.8 ms |
| 8 000 | loads, 13.7 ms |
| 9 000 | **RangeError** |

This board is at 2 636 events. The log is append-only and never pruned, so the ceiling arrives on its own; the write path makes it worse, since `persist` calls `getEdgeRef` per event, which re-reads and re-sorts the whole log.

Fix is an explicit stack in `visit` instead of recursion — the output order must stay identical (pre-order DFS, siblings by ULID). Touches ordering, so `replay-equivalence` and `npm run test:collab` both have to pass.

Found while benchmarking log load for WDZ3VRV.

add.issue.comment.md:
Solution: 5b9bfca1. `resolveEnvActor` (`source/lib/config/actor-env.ts`) reads `EPIQ_USER_NAME` / `EPIQ_USER_ID` and `loadSettingsFromConfig` applies it before its "identity configured?" check, so every surface reading that funnel — TUI boot, GUI init, MCP `getActor` — acts as the environment's actor. `isValidUserId` / `isValidUserName` moved out of `event-persist` into the new module so one definition serves both.

Without a pinned id, the id is sha256(`epiq:actor:<lowercased name>`) rendered in Crockford base32. Actor ids are only compared and used as a file name — nothing calls `decodeTime` on one — so a digest is safe where a ULID would otherwise go.

Verified: unit suite (634) green, `test:collab` green, tsc/eslint/prettier clean. The integration test fails red without the `loadSettingsFromConfig` wiring.
add.issue.comment.author: 01KSAYRA4GHEKJP888WFBWBRDD

add.issue.comment.md:
Solution: option 1 chosen. Agents get their own contributor identity from the environment rather than a ticket prop, a tag, or an assignee convention — implemented in WDZ3VRV. No code change belongs on this ticket; it existed to settle the fork.

Two things the options list did not know, measured while implementing:
- File count costs about 30 µs per file per event write, because `persist` calls `getEdgeRef`, which re-reads and re-sorts the whole log. 4 files: 5.6 ms. 500: 15.6 ms. 2 000: 53 ms. Deriving the id from the name keeps this in the handful-of-files range; per-session ids would not.
- The real ceiling is unrelated to actors: the log stops loading at ~9 000 events. Filed as 1HA2A7XY.

add.issue.comment.md:
Correcting my own severity claim, and folding this together with the far-future-ULID ticket (61G931Z) — they are one problem.

The reorder is real but mostly harmless to the board: the forged root is visited first, then `visit(genesis)` walks the genuine chain intact, so the derived state is unchanged apart from the forged event itself, which materializes against an uninitialized state and is a `materializeSkip`. "Reorders all of history" overstates it.

What actually breaks is every **time-based** view, and that is the same damage 61G931Z does from the other end: `splitEventsAtTime`, `getEventTimeline` and `checkoutStateAt` all cut by `decodeTime(eventId)`. One event dated 1970 (this ticket) or 2126 (61G931Z) stretches the scrubber's range over decades and collapses the real history into a sliver, permanently, for everyone.

That makes the fix a decision rather than a patch, which is why both are now tagged `human-input-needed`:

- Ordering must not consult the wall clock — that is a stated invariant, and `refId` + ULID already handles ordering correctly here.
- Time travel and the scrubber cannot avoid consulting it; that is what they are.
- So the guard has to live in the time-based views, and any bound on "implausible" is either **absolute** (machine-independent, but only catches the extremes) or **relative to now** (catches the realistic cases, but makes the rendered range depend on when you look, so two machines can disagree).

My recommendation: clamp in the *view* layer only — `getEventTimeline` and the scrubber pick their range from a percentile of event times rather than min/max, and `checkoutStateAt` keeps using raw `decodeTime`. Ordering, replay and the derived board stay untouched, so nothing about convergence changes. But it is your call.

The unambiguous half — an id at ULID's ceiling, which made writes fail forever — is fixed and shipped under 1SWDEZA.

Correcting the fix I proposed in this description: capping the *seed* in `persist` would mint an id below its own edge, which the architecture explicitly forbids ("never mint an id without seeding past the current edge"). In practice ordering survives it — the ULID only breaks ties between siblings, and traversal is parent-first from `refId` — but it is a documented invariant, so it is not mine to overrule. Two shapes reach it, and neither can come from a well-behaved writer:

Ordering is unaffected either way — it comes from `refId`, and the ULID only breaks ties between siblings of the same parent.

add.issue.name: MCP tool handlers take no lock, unlike both GUI transports

edit.description.md:
`runExclusive` in `epiq-time-travel.ts` serializes read-then-write over the shared state singleton across an `await`. The GUI HTTP routes take it (`runMutation`) and the WebSocket takes it for every mutating message. **No MCP tool takes it** — `source/mcp/server.ts` is `async input => resultJson(await createIssue(input))` throughout, and `grep runExclusive source/mcp/server.ts source/mcp/epiq-api.ts` finds nothing.

Every `epiq-api` function starts with `boot()`, which calls `resetState()` and re-materializes the whole log into the module singleton, then reads that singleton for its preconditions, then persists. That is a read-modify-write across several awaits with no mutual exclusion.

The MCP SDK does not serialize requests, so two in flight on one server interleave: one call's `boot()` can wipe and rebuild the singleton while another is between its precondition check and its `materializeAndPersistAll`. The precondition was then checked against state that no longer exists — which is exactly the case `runExclusive`'s own comment says "checking then awaiting is check-then-act" about.

This matters more than it looks right now: several agents working one board through one MCP server is the normal case here, and an agent issuing parallel tool calls is the default way to be efficient.

Not yet reproduced — filed from reading, and the race is timing-dependent enough that a test needs to drive two calls concurrently and assert on the persisted log rather than on a returned Result. That test is the first piece of work.

Fix, once confirmed: wrap the tool handlers in the same `runExclusive`, at the `server.registerTool` boundary so it is one change rather than one per function, and check nothing reached from there takes it again — it is not re-entrant.

Found by adversarial stress testing on branch `worktree-security-stress-audit`.

add.issue.comment.md:
Solution: `2380c441` — `WebSocketServer` now takes a `verifyClient` that refuses any handshake whose `Origin` is not one this server serves.

New `source/gui/api/lib/origin-guard.ts` holds `isForeignOrigin(origin, port)`, shared with the HTTP guard (23Z1P5P) so the two transports cannot drift apart. It accepts `127.0.0.1`, `localhost`, `[::1]` and `epiq.localhost` on this server's own bound port, over `http:` only. The port is threaded in as `getPort()` rather than a value, because the handler is built before `listen` resolves it and the preferred 3710 is not always what we get.

A request with **no** `Origin` is allowed. A browser always sends one on a handshake, so "present and not ours" is the entire attack; refusing the absent case would only break curl and the harness, neither of which is the threat — they already have filesystem access to the repo.

Verified against a real `startGuiServer`, before and after:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `Origin: https://evil.example` | accepted, frames dispatched | refused, HTTP 401 |
| `Origin: http://127.0.0.1:9999` | accepted | refused, HTTP 401 |
| `Origin: http://epiq.localhost:<port>` | accepted | accepted |
| no Origin | accepted | accepted |

`websocket-origin.test.ts` covers all four against a live server; `origin-guard.test.ts` covers the matcher, including near-misses that a naive `endsWith` would let through (`notlocalhost`, `evil.epiq.localhost`, `https` on our own port, and the opaque `null` origin a sandboxed iframe sends).

Full Playwright suite passes 44/44 with the guard in place, so the real client is unaffected.

add.issue.comment.md:
Solution: `d024bea3` — every non-GET request to the GUI server passes `refuseCrossSiteRequest` before it reaches a route.

Two gates, because either alone leaves a hole:
- **Origin.** Present and not this server's own loopback origin → 403. Shares `isForeignOrigin` with the WebSocket guard (9VSKT61).
- **Content-type.** A POST that is not `application/json` → 415. This is the half that closes the no-Origin case: `text/plain` is a CORS *simple request*, so the browser sends it with no preflight; requiring JSON forces a preflight this server never answers.

Kept out of the closure and put in `origin-guard.ts` so it is unit-testable — the first draft was an inline helper inside `startGuiServer` and could only be reached through a live server.

Verified against a real `startGuiServer`:

| request | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| POST `text/plain` + evil Origin | reached the handler | 403 |
| POST `application/json` + evil Origin | reached the handler | 403 |
| POST `text/plain`, no Origin | reached the handler | 415 |
| POST `application/json` + own Origin | reached the handler | reached the handler |
| GET `/api/state` | 200 | 200 |

The client already sent `content-type: application/json` on its one POST (`/api/attachments`), and its DELETEs carry no body, so nothing needed changing there. Full Playwright suite passes 44/44.

add.issue.name: Make ticket refs in comments and descriptions clickable

edit.description.md:
Refs get mentioned constantly in comments and descriptions — "Filed `QDNP1JS` from a code selection", "filed under 2Q1QAPB", the story tickets' own "Broken into" lists — and every one of them is dead text you have to go find by hand.

Linkify them so a click opens that ticket.

**Only linkify refs that actually resolve to a ticket.** A ref is 7 Crockford-base32 characters, which is not a shape you can distinguish from prose or a short sha by pattern alone (`SEGMENT` matches; a lowercase sha doesn't, but an uppercase one would). `findIssue` already resolves a ref across every board, so the known-ref set is free — matching against it removes the false-positive problem entirely rather than trying to out-clever it with a regex.

Handle both bare refs in prose and refs written as inline code, since both forms are already in use. Never rewrite inside an existing link (nested links are invalid, and an explicit link's text is the author's own label).

add.issue.comment.md:
Solution: `75b1425f` — `source/gui/api/lib/websocket.schema.ts` parses every frame against a zod discriminated union, replacing `JSON.parse(raw) as GuiMessage`.

**A worse bug than this ticket described, found while writing it.** Handlers do `{repoRoot, ...message.payload}` — the spread comes second, so it *wins*. A frame carrying its own `repoRoot` key pointed the mutation at a different epiq project on the machine. Twenty handlers, one line each. `z.object` drops unknown keys, so parsing closes all twenty at once; there is a test asserting a smuggled `repoRoot` is stripped.

Also fixed by the same change: `targetTime`/`start`/`end` are `z.number().finite()`, so `NaN` and `±Infinity` no longer reach `checkoutStateAt` or the timeline bucketing; a missing or wrong-typed payload is now a refusal rather than an internal TypeError echoed to the client.

A compile-time assertion checks `z.infer<typeof GuiMessageSchema> extends GuiMessage`, so the schema cannot drift from the transport it validates without failing the build.

The two `if (!message.payload.issueId) return 'Missing issueId'` guards in `issue:close` / `issue:reopen` are gone — the schema guarantees it, so they were dead. The `position` guards stay: `position` is genuinely optional.

Full Playwright suite passes 44/44, which is the real proof the schema still accepts everything the client sends.

add.issue.name: Sync commits whatever is on disk, so a damaged log becomes permanent shared history

edit.description.md:
**This one actually happened, today, on this board.**

At 18:26:56 commit `d4cbd0b3` took `.epiq/events/01ksayra4ghekjp888wfbwbrdd.jola.jsonl` from **2158 lines to 1** and pushed it. Every clone that pulled lost the board. Recovered by hand from `d4cbd0b3^` (restored at `0288a99d`, 2175 lines, derived board byte-identical to before).

It had happened three times before unnoticed — a few lines each in June (`2617b871`, `6a81a4af`, `21a8b691`, and four more).

## What the evidence shows

- The state worktree's reflog is **pure `commit:` entries** — no `checkout:`, `reset:`, `pull:` or `rebase:`. Nobody ran git in there by hand.
- The truncating commit carries epiq's own `[sync|branch:…|sha:…]` message and touches exactly the one pathspec `stageStateBranchOwnEventFile` stages. It was made by the sync path, not a person.
- The single surviving line was a freshly minted `create.contributor` — what `ensureContributorCurrent` writes as the *first* event into an **empty** log. So the file was already gone from disk before the commit; the sync faithfully committed what it found.

So the destructive act was a filesystem write, and the code turned it into permanent, replicated, append-only-unrecoverable damage. Which process emptied the file is not provable from what is in git, and I am not going to guess — but it does not matter for this ticket. Any process that can write to the worktree can do it, and several do: the MCP server, the GUI's autosync, a dev server, a test run. Note `01ksayra4ghekjp888wfbwbrdd.test.jsonl` (529 lines) sitting in the real state branch — test runs have been writing into production state.

## The gap

"Never rewrite, reorder or de-duplicate existing log lines" is a documented invariant with **zero enforcement**. `createStateBranchSyncCommit` commits the file as it sits. One bad working copy plus one autosync is all it takes, and autosync fires every ~30s.

## Fix

Before staging, compare the working copy against `HEAD:<path>`; if any committed line is gone, refuse the whole sync and say so. Checked *before* staging so a damaged log never reaches the index. Lines may be added and reordered freely (order is derived from `refId`); only loss is refused.

Deliberately not auto-healing. The missing lines are recoverable from git, but silently rewriting a log the user did not ask us to touch is how this happened in the first place.

add.issue.name: An event ordered before init.workspace crashes every client on load

edit.description.md:
Found by the new adversarial collab suite (RYTZFJV) — it earned its keep on the first run.

`getState()` throws `'State not initialized. Call initWorkspaceState() first.'`. Every materializer reaches it through `nodeRepo`. Any event that sorts **ahead of `init.workspace`** therefore runs against no state and throws, and the throw is uncaught all the way out of `materializeAll` — so the process dies on load rather than skipping one event.

Two ways to get there, both one appended line:
- a forged root (`refId: null`) with a low ULID (Y76V1ZY)
- an id that is not a decodable ULID, which sorts before every real one

Reproduced end to end over real git sync: a peer publishes such a line, and the other machine's process exits 1 with the stack through `lockNode → getNode → getState`. That is worse than the truncation class of bug — it is an uncaught crash, permanent, and it reaches everyone who pulls.

This raises Y76V1ZY's real severity: I had downgraded it to "distorts the timeline". It also crashes the board.

## Fix

Guard in `materialize()`: if the state is not initialized and the action is not `init.workspace`, return `materializeSkip`. That is precisely what the architecture asks for — "make it idempotent, express preconditions as `materializeSkip` rather than fatal" — and one place covers every handler.

Also worth doing separately: `getState()` throwing at all is the root hazard, and `getSafeState()` already exists. Auditing the other callers is its own ticket.

add.issue.comment.md:
Solution: `564a4e19` — `assertLogOnlyGrew` in the new `source/git/log-integrity.ts`, called from `stageStateBranchOwnEventFile` **before** anything is staged.

It reads `HEAD:<relative path>` and refuses the sync if any committed line is absent from the working copy. Lines may be added freely, and reordering is fine — order is derived from `refId`, so only *loss* is a defect. The refusal names the file, how many of how many events went missing, quotes the first one, and points at `git show HEAD:<path>` for recovery.

Placed before staging on purpose: a damaged log must not reach the index, or an autosync a second later commits it.

Deliberately not auto-healing. The missing lines are sitting in git and it is tempting, but silently rewriting a log nobody asked us to touch is the shape of the original bug.

Verified red first: with the guard removed, both truncation tests fail. `log-integrity.test.ts` covers the pure diff (append, reorder, blank lines, missing trailing newline, single drop, wholesale truncation) and drives the real `stageStateBranchOwnEventFile` against a real two-commit repo — including asserting the index is left **empty** after a refusal, so there is nothing for a concurrent sync to pick up. First-sync-with-no-committed-version is allowed.

Not covered by this, and worth their own tickets: whatever wrote the bad working copy in the first place, and the fact that `01ksayra4ghekjp888wfbwbrdd.test.jsonl` shows test runs writing into the real state branch.

add.issue.name: Test runs write into the real state branch

edit.description.md:
`.epiq/events/01ksayra4ghekjp888wfbwbrdd.test.jsonl` — **529 lines**, sitting in the live state branch. Same actor ULID as the real identity, display name `test`. Test runs have been writing events into production state, and those events are committed, pushed and replayed on every client like any other.

`no-git-outside-tmp.ts` already exists and is good: it fails any test that points **git** at a directory outside `$TMPDIR`, and its own comment says it was written because "a test run once rewrote the developer's branches and git identity". But it only guards `git`. It does not guard `EPIQ_GLOBAL_DIR`, and that is where the state worktree lives — so a test that resolves the real global dir writes real event files without ever running git outside tmp.

This is the same class of accident as the truncation (8PYTCM), and plausibly connected: the more processes writing to the real state worktree, the more chances one leaves it in a state a sync then publishes.

## Fix

Extend the existing setup file, since it is the chokepoint every suite already shares:
- fail any test where `getGlobalConfigDir()` resolves outside `$TMPDIR`, the same way `assertThrowaway` does for git cwd
- default `EPIQ_GLOBAL_DIR` to a per-run temp dir in `setupFiles` so a suite that forgets is isolated rather than failed

Then decide what to do about the 529 lines already in the log. They are append-only history, so removing them means rewriting the branch — probably not worth it, but the events are visible on the board and somebody should look at whether they are noise.

Found while investigating the log truncation on branch `worktree-security-stress-audit`.

add.issue.comment.md:
Solution: `83c0f40a` — `materialize()` returns `materializeSkip` when the state is not initialized and the action is not `init.workspace`.

One guard at the top of `materialize`, before the handler runs, so it covers every action rather than the handful that happen to reach `getState()` first. Wording of the skip names the action, so the log says which event arrived early rather than just that something did.

add.issue.name: Relocating the state worktree force-deletes unsynced events and reports success

edit.description.md:
Reproduced. This is the closest thing yet to a mechanism for the 8PYTCM incident.

`ensureStateBranchWorktree` (`source/git/git.ts`):

```ts
if (existing && existing !== expected) {
    logger.info('Moving state branch worktree to expected location');
    await git.worktreeRemove({cwd: repoRoot, worktreeRoot: existing});
}
```

`worktreeRemove` passes `--force`, which is exactly the flag that overrides git's refusal to delete a worktree holding uncommitted work. The state worktree is *almost always* holding some: every `persist` appends to the log and nothing commits until the next sync.

`expected` is `$EPIQ_GLOBAL_DIR/worktrees/<projectId>`. So the two paths disagree the moment two processes resolve `EPIQ_GLOBAL_DIR` differently — a dev server, a test run, an agent with its own environment, anything started from a different shell. The loser's unsynced events are deleted outright. There is no stash and no reflog for a removed worktree; they are simply gone.

And this is not a rare path: `bootstrapStateBranchStorage` calls it, and `boot()` calls that — so **every MCP tool call, every GUI request and every sync goes through it.**

Worse than the deletion: it returned **success**. The caller carried on and the next `persist` recreated the log from empty, which is precisely the one-line file found at the scene of the truncation.

Repro in `worktree-move-data-loss.test.ts`: create the worktree at path A, append an unsynced line, call `ensureStateBranchWorktree` with path B. Before the fix the line is gone and the call succeeds.

## Fix

Check `git status --porcelain --untracked-files=all` in the existing worktree first and refuse the relocation if anything is uncommitted, naming both paths and saying to sync from the other location first. Untracked counts: a contributor's first log is untracked until their first sync, so ignoring it would miss the events most easily lost.

A clean worktree still relocates — that behaviour is legitimate and is covered by its own test.

Found by adversarial stress testing on branch `worktree-fatal-state-audit`.

add.issue.name: A broken worktree path is rm -rf'd with its event logs still in it

edit.description.md:
Sibling of 2WFGV2, on the same code path.

`createStateBranchWorktree` (`source/git/git.ts`):

```ts
if (fs.existsSync(stateBranchRoot) && !fs.existsSync(path.join(stateBranchRoot, '.git'))) {
    logger.info('Removing broken state branch worktree path');
    removePath(stateBranchRoot);   // fs.rmSync(recursive, force)
}
```

A worktree missing its `.git` pointer is broken, but broken is not empty — the event logs are still sitting in it. And missing `.git` is exactly the case where there is **no committed copy at that path to recover them from**, so this is the one deletion in the codebase that no git object survives. Everything else that goes wrong with the log is recoverable because git is content-addressed; this is not.

How a worktree ends up with logs and no `.git`: another process pruned the registration, a copy of the directory, an interrupted `worktree add`, or the force-removal in 2WFGV2 racing a `persist` that recreates the events dir underneath it.

## Fix

Before deleting, scan `.epiq/events` for `.jsonl` files with content. If any, refuse and name them, telling the user to move the directory aside and salvage the logs. Empty files do not block — refusing over one would strand the cleanup that unblocks the user. An unreadable directory also refuses: unreadable is not "safe to delete".

Covered in `worktree-move-data-loss.test.ts`, verified red without the guard.

Found by adversarial stress testing on branch `worktree-fatal-state-audit`.

add.issue.name: Sync aborts an in-flight rebase before checking whether one is in flight

edit.description.md:
Real ordering bug, but the fix is a trade-off I am not going to make alone — I tried it and the test suite pushed back for a good reason.

## The bug

`ensureSyncReady` (`source/git/sync.ts`) runs in this order:

1. `bootstrapStateBranchStorage(...)` — which reaches `ensureStateBranchCheckedOut`, and that runs **`git rebase --abort`** in the state worktree whenever `getCurrentBranch` is not the state branch
2. `hasInProgressGitOperation(stateBranchRoot)` — refuse if a git operation is in progress

Mid-rebase, HEAD is detached, so step 1's branch check does not match and the abort fires. A concurrent sync's rebase looks identical to a stale one and gets aborted out from under it. Step 2 exists to prevent exactly that and runs *after* the damage.

`syncEpiqWithRemote` rebases with `rebase.autoStash=true`, so an abort mid-rebase can also leave events sitting in a stash nobody looks at.

## Why I did not just reorder it

Moving the check before bootstrap makes `git-machines.test.ts > recovers from a stale rebase left behind by an earlier interrupted sync` fail — deliberately. That blind abort is the recovery path for a sync killed mid-rebase. Reorder it and a single crash leaves the state branch permanently unsyncable until somebody runs git by hand, which for an agent-driven board is arguably worse than the race.

So the two failure modes trade off directly:

| | today | after a naive reorder |
|---|---|---|
| concurrent sync mid-rebase | aborted, work may be stashed and lost | refused, both survive |
| sync crashed mid-rebase | recovers by itself | stuck until manual intervention |

## Options

1. **Distinguish stale from live by age.** Abort only if the rebase state directory has not been touched for N seconds; refuse otherwise. Cheap and matches how the rest of the code reasons (timeouts everywhere), but N is a guess and a slow rebase on a big log could be misjudged.
2. **A real lock**: pid + heartbeat file in the worktree, abort only when the holder is gone. Correct, and the only option that actually knows the answer. More machinery, and needs a stale-lock story of its own.
3. **Reorder and accept manual recovery**, with a clear error naming `git rebase --abort` as the fix.

My preference is 2, with 1 as the cheap interim — but with several agents syncing one board every ~30s this decides how the system behaves under exactly the conditions that produced the 8PYTCM incident, so it is yours.

Found by adversarial stress testing on branch `worktree-fatal-state-audit`.

add.issue.comment.md:

New `hasUncommittedChanges` in `git-utils.ts` uses `git status --porcelain --untracked-files=all`. **Untracked is the important half**: a contributor's first event log is untracked until their first sync, so a check that only looked at tracked changes would miss exactly the events most easily lost.

The refusal names both paths and says what to do — sync from the other location, or point both at the same `EPIQ_GLOBAL_DIR` — because the cause is always a configuration disagreement, not a git problem.

Verified red first: with the guard removed, the unsynced line is gone and the call returns success. A clean worktree still relocates, covered by its own case so the guard cannot quietly disable a legitimate move.

Note this is a *refusal*, not a safe relocation. Moving the worktree while preserving uncommitted events would mean committing them first, and committing on somebody else's behalf during what is meant to be a bootstrap step is a bigger decision than this fix should make. Refusing is the conservative half; if the refusal turns out to be common in practice, doing the move properly is a follow-up.

add.issue.comment.md:
Solution: `abb836e1` — took option 2 from the description, the pid + heartbeat lock. New `source/git/sync-lock.ts`, acquired at `syncEpiqWithRemote` and nowhere else.

**Why this and not the reorder:** it is the only option that keeps *both* properties. The reorder (option 3) traded the race for a permanent lockout after any crash; a timeout (option 1) guesses. Liveness is a fact the OS will answer.

The decision table the code now implements:

| lock file | holder | action |
|---|---|---|
| absent | — | proceed |
| present, pid dead | crashed | break it, abort the rebase, recover |
| present, pid alive | live sync | refuse, report a skip |

Proof it gets both halves: `git-machines.test.ts > recovers from a stale rebase left behind by an earlier interrupted sync` passes **unchanged**. That is the test that vetoed the reorder, and it still passes because a crashed process leaves no live lock.

## Mechanics

- Acquire is one `writeFileSync(..., {flag: 'wx'})` — the check and the claim are a single syscall, so two processes cannot both win. `process.kill(pid, 0)` tests liveness; `EPERM` counts as alive (another user's process, emphatically not ours to break).
- The lock lives in the **gitdir**, never the worktree tree — nothing here may ever become committable, and `.epiq/` is staged by glob.
- Held elsewhere returns a *skip*, not a failure (`skipped` on `SyncSummary`). Autosync contends constantly; an error every few seconds would be noise, and nothing touches sync state on a skip so the indicator stays truthful.
- Taken at one chokepoint deliberately. Sprinkling it per-caller is exactly how `runExclusive` ended up covering the GUI transports but not the MCP tools.

## Limits, recorded rather than papered over

- **Advisory.** Binds epiq processes, not a person running git in the worktree. Git's own `index.lock` / `rebase-merge/` remain the hard boundary.
- **Pid reuse** can make a dead holder look alive. `STALE_AFTER_MS` (10 min) is the backstop. Note the failure direction is *refuse*, not *destroy* — the safe way to be wrong, which is the main argument for this over a timeout.
- **Local filesystem assumed.** `pid` is meaningless across hosts and `wx` is not reliably atomic on NFS, so a foreign `hostname` is never broken on liveness — only on age.
- **First sync is unlocked.** There is no worktree to hold before bootstrap creates one. Two processes racing a project's very first sync is a narrower window and is not covered here.

Nine tests in `sync-lock.test.ts`, including three concurrent callers asserting peak concurrency is exactly 1.

Not done here, deliberately: extending the lock to serialise the MCP tool handlers. It would subsume that ticket, but widening this change past sync is how a scoped fix turns into an unreviewable one.

add.issue.name: Contributor namespace grows one permanent entry per agent session

edit.description.md:
Naming a session after its worktree (`claude/tag-filter`) means one new contributor per worktree, forever. 3. **Fixed pool of session names** (`claude/1..4`, reused). Bounded by construction, zero code, but the name stops saying what the session was doing.

Naming a session `claude/tag-filter` smuggles two different things into one string: **who** (claude) and **what** (tag-filter). "Who" is a small set; "what" is unbounded — which is exactly why the contributor registry grows without limit (01M17EDR). add.issue.name: Return ref from every response that carries a node id

edit.description.md:
Only four sites in `epiq-api.ts` emit `ref` (lines 368, 420, 1115, 1130) and every one is a list/read path. Every **mutation** returns a bare `id`: `createIssue`, `moveIssue`, `closeIssue`, `reopenIssue`, `editIssueTitle`, `editIssueDescription`, `createSwimlane`, `editSwimlaneTitle`, `moveSwimlane`, `deleteSwimlane`, `addIssueComment`, `addIssueTag`, `addIssueAssignee`.

That is exactly the wrong moment to withhold it. Right after `epiq_issue_create` is when the caller writes the ref-prefixed commit, and the response gives them everything except the one field they need — so they reconstruct it from the id and get it wrong.

Concretely: four commits reached main this session with truncated refs (`8PYTCM` for `B8PYTCM`, `51H3F1` for `F51H3F1`, `2WFGV2` for `E2WFGV2`, `1TCS14` for `W1TCS14`), because `id.slice(-7)` done by eye drops a character.

Rule: **any response carrying a node `id` also carries `nodeRef(id)`.** One line per return site.

This removes the temptation but not the possibility — the enforcement half is the `commit-msg` hook ticket.</description>

add.issue.name: A wrong commit ref fails silently forever — add a commit-msg hook

edit.description.md:
The reason refs keep going wrong is not carelessness, it is that **nothing ever says they are wrong.**

`getCommitsForRef` matches with:

```ts
const prefix = `${ref.toUpperCase()} `;
commit.subject.toUpperCase().startsWith(prefix)
```

An exact 7-character prefix. So `8PYTCM` where the ref is `B8PYTCM` matches nothing — the ticket shows zero commits, forever, and no error, warning or test ever mentions it. There is no feedback loop to learn from, which is why the same mistake recurs.

There is no `commit-msg` hook at all today; `.husky/` has only `pre-push`.

## What it should do

Not "every commit must carry a ref" — main has plenty of legitimate ref-less commits (`epiq skill: never test against the real board`, `make ticket refs in comments and descriptions clickable`). Enforcing presence would be wrong.

Instead: **if the leading token looks like a ref, it must resolve.**

- token equals a known node ref → pass
- token is Crockford-shaped and a strict substring of exactly one known ref → **reject**, and name the full ref. This is the truncation case and it is high-confidence.
- token is exactly 7 Crockford characters and matches nothing → reject as a probable typo
- anything else → pass

Crockford base32 excludes I, L, O and U, which knocks out most English words and keeps false positives low.

## Failure behaviour

Fail **open** when the board cannot be read — a missing state worktree or an unreadable log must never block committing. Fail **closed** only when a token genuinely looks like a ref and does not resolve. Skip merges, `fixup!`/`squash!`, reverts and epiq's own `[epiq:*]` commits.

The pure decision belongs in testable code, with the hook as a thin wrapper — including a regression test that a truncated ref is rejected, which is the test this whole class of mistake never had.

add.issue.name: No way to fetch one issue by id or ref

edit.description.md:
There is no `epiq_issue_get`. To go from a ref back to a ticket — the inverse of the commit-prefix convention — you have to `epiq_issue_list` the whole board and filter client-side.

That is not academic: `epiq_issue_list` on this board now returns ~160 KB, over the MCP response cap, so it spills to a file that then has to be parsed just to read one field. It happened three times in one session, twice only to look up a `ref`.

Wanted: `epiq_issue_get({idOrRef})` returning the single issue with `id`, `ref`, title, description, parent, tags, assignees.

- accepts a full ULID or a 7-character ref, case-insensitive
- an ambiguous ref (matches more than one) fails and lists the candidates rather than guessing — `nodeRefMatches` is a *substring* match, so short input genuinely can be ambiguous
- unknown id or ref fails plainly

Pairs with the "return ref everywhere" ticket: one gives you the ref when you create, this gives you the ticket when all you have is the ref.

add.issue.name: State-branch push runs the host repo's husky pre-push hook and fails

edit.description.md:
`epiq_sync` fails at "state branch push" with `npm error Missing script: "lint:err"`. The state worktree is a worktree of the host repo, so it inherits `core.hooksPath = .husky/_`; `git push` there runs the repo's pre-push hook (lint, typecheck, tests, containers) in a directory with no package.json scripts. Reproduces on every sync since 28dc16d6 (FV6VS2M, 2026-08-29) put the container run in pre-push — any earlier push would have failed the same way for lint:err, so the trigger is likely husky's `prepare` having installed the hooks path recently.

Fix: the sync's pull/push of the state branch should run with `--no-verify` (or `-c core.hooksPath=/dev/null`) — hooks belong to the code branches, not the event log.

Until then local board changes queue up unpushed.

add.issue.name: getCommitsForRef accepts a wrong-length ref and silently returns nothing

edit.description.md:
`getCommitsForRef` validates only that the ref is non-empty, then does a strict 7-character prefix match against commit subjects. Hand it a 6- or 8-character ref and it returns an empty list with no complaint — indistinguishable from "this ticket has no commits yet".

A ref is `NODE_REF_LENGTH` (7) characters by construction. Any other length is a certain mistake, not a legitimate query, and saying so turns a silent empty result into an answer.

Also worth noting a real inconsistency while in here: `nodeRefMatches` (board filtering) is a **substring** match, so `zcs5` finds a node, while commit linking is a **strict prefix**. Two matching rules for one concept. That gap is part of why a truncated ref feels like it works — it still finds the ticket in the UI while the commit link silently does not. Either align them or document the split deliberately.

add.issue.comment.md:
Revising this: the mechanism it needs now exists, so the work is smaller than the description implies.

W1TCS14 shipped `source/git/sync-lock.ts` — a cross-process lock keyed on pid + hostname + start time, acquired with an atomic `wx` write, broken automatically when the holder is gone. It is taken at `syncEpiqWithRemote` and nowhere else, deliberately, precisely so it does not get sprinkled per-caller the way `runExclusive` was.

So this ticket is no longer "design a locking story for MCP". It is: decide whether MCP tool handlers take that same lock, and at which boundary.

Two things that have not changed, and one that has:

- **Still true:** no MCP tool takes `runExclusive`. `source/mcp/server.ts` is still `async input => resultJson(await createIssue(input))` throughout.
- **Still true:** this was filed from reading and has **never been reproduced**. Any work here should start with a test driving two tool calls concurrently and asserting on the persisted log, not on a returned Result. Without that, a fix cannot be shown to fix anything.
- **Changed:** the sync lock is process-level and file-based, so it composes with an MCP handler in a way an in-process promise chain does not. If the handlers take it, one mechanism covers both this and W1TCS14, which is the strongest argument for doing it.

One caution against reaching for `sync-lock` directly: it is a *sync* lock over the state worktree, and MCP handlers contend over the in-process state singleton, which is a different resource with a different lifetime. Using one lock for both is defensible but is a decision, not an obvious refactor — worth stating explicitly in whichever direction it goes.

add.issue.name: Read-side consumers trust decodeTime() of a poisoned id

edit.description.md:
Follow-up to 61G931Z, from the review of branch `fix-61g931z`. The mint-side clamp stops a far-future edge from dragging future ids forward, but an already-poisoned id in the log stays poisoned (append-only), and several readers trust `decodeTime(id)` as fact:

- `replay-engine.ts` `buildPlaybackFractions`: one astronomical gap swallows the whole [0,1] budget — replay becomes a dead pause then a last-frame dump.
- `splitEventsAtTime`: the poisoned event (and, via the causal cascade, everything after it) never satisfies `decodeTime < targetTime`, so historical checkouts near it hide more than expected.
- `epiq-time-travel.ts` `getEventTimeline`: a far-future `t` falls outside every window ending at now — the event vanishes from the GUI scrubber silently.
- `CommentListUI` sorts comments by `decodeTime(id)`; a poisoned comment sorts to the far end with a nonsense "time ago".
- `PeekStatus` decodes the edge id for the status bar — can show a date a century out.

Options: clamp at the display/read boundary (one helper, N call sites), or quarantine/flag far-future ids at ingest the way `corrupt-line`/`unsupported-schema-version` already are (heavier; touches ordering semantics — needs care with "unreadable stays ordered").

Damage limited to logs that already contain a poisoned id; the mint guard prevents new ones.

add.issue.name: A log line with two action keys hard-fails the whole board load instead of being quarantined

edit.description.md:
Found by a verification agent during the review of branch `worktree-fix-v0yqdxv` (V0YQDXV clamp commit); pre-existing, not introduced by that diff.

A crafted line carrying two action keys (e.g. both `evil.event` and `init.workspace`) passes `PersistedEnvelopeSchema` (only `v` + `id` are validated, extra keys preserved), so it enters the sort set rather than the `corrupt-line` quarantine. Decode then rejects it in `getPersistedAction` ("expected exactly 1 action key") — and `decodeReconstructedEvents` propagates that as a hard failure of the entire load (`event-load.ts:208-216`).

With `merge=union` and append-only logs, one such line pushed by any peer permanently bricks the board for every client that pulls it — same class as CB211FF, which quarantined unparseable lines for exactly this reason.

Fix direction: treat "not exactly one action key" the way `corrupt-line`/`unsupported-schema-version` are treated — quarantine at ingest, keep the envelope ordered ("unreadable stays ordered"), never fail the whole decode.

add.issue.name: Root filter checks only key presence, so a forged line with an init.workspace key still front-runs history

edit.description.md:
From the review of branch `worktree-fix-v0yqdxv`; pre-existing on main, not introduced by that branch. Sibling of 7GBW8QW (the two-action-key hard-fail).

The anti-forgery root filter in `getSortedEvents` admits any `refId: null` event where `'init.workspace' in event` (`event-load.ts` roots filter). The loose envelope schema preserves extra keys, so a hand-written line `{"v":1,"id":["00000000000000000000000000",null],"init.workspace":{...}}` passes the filter and its all-zero ULID sorts ahead of the real genesis — restoring the reordering the filter exists to prevent. The existing test only exercises an `evil.event` root, the case the filter happens to catch. `initWorkspaceState` also rebuilds state wholesale with no already-initialized guard.

Fix direction: require exactly one payload key equal to `init.workspace`, and skip a second genesis at materialization.

add.issue.name: epiq_sync holds the MCP lock across the whole network sync, starving reads

edit.description.md:
From the review of branch `worktree-fix-v0yqdxv`; pre-existing on main, not introduced by that branch.

`exclusiveTool(sync)` in `source/mcp/server.ts` holds the single unbounded FIFO for the full fetch/rebase/push cycle — 10s per subprocess but no aggregate bound, so a slow or unreachable remote can hold it 40–100s across retries. Every read tool (previously instant from materialized state) queues behind it and can exceed the MCP client's tool timeout.

The lock itself is necessary (sync rewrites the state-branch worktree that boot() reads). Hardening options: a runExclusive timeout, or scoping sync's hold to the state-mutating window.

add.issue.comment.md:
Review of the branch found the second half of this ticket unimplemented: the root filter alone does not close the hole.

A forged root carrying *only* `init.workspace` satisfies the new "exactly one action key" filter by construction. Give it a high ULID and it anchors after real history, so `materialize` re-runs genesis part-way through replay — `initWorkspaceState` rebuilds state wholesale, discarding every event applied before it. One crafted line empties the board on every clone that pulls it.

Fixed in c67b7a28: `ReplayBatch` carries a `genesisApplied` flag, and a second `init.workspace` within a replay is a `materializeSkip` rather than a reset. The guard is per batch, not on `isStateInitialized()`, because `_appState` is never cleared between replays — a global check would skip the real genesis on every reload after the first.

Regression test in `event-materialize.test.ts` ("skips a second genesis rather than resetting the board"), verified red without the fix (workspace node undefined).

add.issue.comment.md:
The pre-push gate caught a regression this ticket's own commit introduced: `peek.e2e.test.ts` failed with ":peek prev — No previous event to peek".

Cause: `loadEffectiveEventTimes` keys its map by the persisted `id[0]`, but peek looks up `getState().eventLog.at(-1)?.id`. Those are two different id spaces for any event created in the current session — the in-memory event carries the ULID minted when it was built, while the log carries the edge-chained id `persist` assigned it (visible in the debug dump: ten in-memory ids all sharing one millisecond, against ten persisted ids each one increment apart). The lookup therefore missed on every freshly created event and peek reported nothing to step to. It only worked after a reload, when persisted ids are back in state.

Fixed in bf54eb30: the lookup falls back to the event's own (clamped) time when the log has no entry for its id. Post-reload the map still supplies the effective time, so the poisoned-id behaviour this ticket is about is unchanged.

Worth noting the existing unit tests could not have caught it — they mock `loadEffectiveEventTimes` to return a map containing exactly the id under test, so the lookup always hits. Added "falls back to the event own time when the log has no entry for its id", verified red without the fix.

Solution: fixed in 755c9897 + 65a2e716 + b589e482 (PR #159, rebase-merged to main).

Chose the read-boundary clamp over quarantine-at-ingest, so ordering semantics are untouched:

add.issue.name: Drag-to-zoom is unreliable on the Events scatter: the canvas cannot tell a click from a drag

edit.description.md:
Follow-up to TVWQZ8S. Dragging out a range works on the Volume chart but poorly on the Events scatter, because `ScatterCanvas` has no notion of a deliberate click versus a drag.

Two faults, both in `ScrubberParts.tsx`:

1. `onPointerDown` calls `stopPropagation()` when the press lands on a commit dot, so the press never reaches the track and no range drag begins at all. In a dense scatter a good share of drags silently die.
2. `onClick` hit-tests at the *release* position, and a `click` fires whenever press and release are both inside the canvas however far apart. So a range drag that happens to end over a commit dot zooms *and* opens that commit's diff.

Fix: settle the gesture on release by distance travelled, the way the track already does with `MIN_RANGE_DRAG_PX`, and open the commit that was *pressed* rather than whatever sits under the release.

P4H5XH was a crash-on-render that every suite missed, because none of them exercises the conditions it needed.

- playwright's global-setup spawns the server through tsx with IS_LOCAL=true, so the browser tests run the source path. The SEA path (`sea.getAsset`) and the packaged dist path are never opened in a browser.
- The e2e suite drives dist/index.js as a TUI, never the GUI.

Work:

1. ~~A browser test that loads the GUI in a repo with no .epiq project.~~ **Done** in `5X9MA0H` — the playwright harness serves a project-less directory beside the seeded repo (`bareUrl` / `bareRepoRoot` in `serve.ts`, `handoff.ts`, `fixtures.ts`), and `init-project.pw.ts` loads the GUI there and asserts it rendered with no page errors.
2. ~~A smoke test against the built dist rather than tsx.~~ **Done** — `dist-build.pw.ts` + `serve-dist.ts`.
3. ~~Something covering the SEA asset path, if it can be made cheap enough to run.~~ **Done** — the SEA build verifies itself; see the Solution comment for why it lives there rather than in a suite.

add.issue.comment.md:
Solution: items 2 and 3 done on `DSBC69B-packaged-gui-tests` (55fe6117, 045db289).

**2 — built dist in a browser.** `dist-build.pw.ts` opens a GUI served by `dist/index.js` itself. `serve-dist.ts` spawns the built CLI with `epiq gui` over the worker's already-seeded repo, drops `IS_LOCAL` (so the client resolves from `dist/gui` beside the bundle, not from cwd) and points `EPIQ_GLOBAL_DIR` at the seed's temp dir — that last one is why `globalDir` is now on the handoff. Two assertions: the board renders with no page errors, and nothing the page requests 404s. Spawned per-file in `beforeAll`, not in `serve.ts`, so only this file pays for the extra process. `epiq gui` opens a browser on start, so the child gets a PATH with no-op `open`/`xdg-open` shims in front — no production change.

Verified red: with `dist/gui/main.js` moved aside, both tests fail.

**3 — SEA asset path.** Not a suite: building a binary is a ~2 minute, ~100MB step, too much for the pre-push gate or per-push CI. Instead `build-sea.mjs` verifies itself in step 7, next to the existing `--version` check — it boots `epiq gui` from the freshly built binary in a temp dir and fetches every asset `index.html` references, so `sea.getAsset` is exercised for real. Costs seconds on a build that already takes minutes, skipped on the cross-build leg (as `--version` already is).

Verified red: renaming the blob's asset prefix from `gui/` to `guix/` fails the build with `GET / served 404`.

Known limit: that only runs where a binary is built — `npm run build:binary`, i.e. the tagged release jobs. A SEA-asset regression is caught at release, not on the PR that causes it. Buying more than that means building a binary per push.

Full playwright suite: 62 passed. Typecheck and lint clean.
